item.title: It never ends...
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: After talking up this summit for months on end, it ended with no real accomplishments, and certainly not with the results Trump had hoped for. He had wanted to discuss the war in Iran and nuclear weapons, but the three men left without announcing any agreement to end the fighting or reduce their nuclear arsenals. They did, however, manage to agree on something else. Trump, Xi, and Putin issued a joint declaration that called for protecting government officials from prosecution and limiting the power of the International Criminal Court, the court responsible for prosecuting some of the world’s worst crimes, including war crimes. Of all the things these three men could have agreed on, one of them was protecting government leaders from international prosecution. That is telling, although hardly surprising coming from them...This morning, inside the Dirksen Senate Office Building, Michael LoSapio, Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is the agency responsible for helping protect American elections from cyberattacks and foreign interference, was asked a question that should have been incredibly easy to answer. Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut wanted to know whether the United States Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021. LoSapio said no, “I don’t believe it was an attack.” When Blumenthal pushed him further, LoSapio responded by claiming, “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.” Then Blumenthal asked him who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election. Again, LoSapio refused to acknowledge what happened. “I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” he said. The man Donald Trump wants to put in charge of the federal agency responsible for helping protect our elections refused to acknowledge that the Capitol was attacked on January 6, and then refused to say who won the popular vote in 2020. Blumenthal looked at him and said, “You are disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill.”He was not the only one today to deny or downplay what happened on January 6. Michael Chamberlain, who Donald Trump nominated to lead the Office of Government Ethics, the people who are supposed to hold public officials accountable, was asked the same question about January 6. He called it “behavior they shouldn’t have.” But he would not call it an attack or an insurrection, or even acknowledge what actually happened that day when a mob stormed the Capitol in an attempt to overturn an election...During a separate hearing, just the day before, this time for a lifetime appointment to the federal judiciary, James P. Sullivan, a sitting justice on the Texas Supreme Court whom Donald Trump nominated to become a federal district judge in Texas, was asked whether Donald Trump could constitutionally run for president again in 2028. Sullivan initially struggled to even remember what the Twenty-second Amendment said, and Senator Chris Coons of Delaware had to help him. As Coons explained, the Twenty-second Amendment is very clear. It says a president who has been elected twice cannot be elected again. But when Coons asked Sullivan whether that meant Trump could not run again, Sullivan would not answer and called it an ongoing political debate. Senator Chris Coons told him, “That’s a very disappointing answer.”

item.title: Maryos Syawish
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something slightly more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Maryos Syawish, an Iraqi electronic musician based in Naarm/Melbourne. He’s one half of the duo Sleep D, who we recommended back in 2020. His new record, , has been in the works for about eight years, mixing field recordings from his home country with synths and drum machines. Assummarized, there’s “meditative, shimmering atmospheres… stuttering, breakbeat-infected downtempo… wormhole-traversing electronics… and billowing, cinematic drone.” We’re also playing Sleep D’s 2019 LP, , which is more of a traditional Friday four-on-the-floor.

item.title: The Day the President Moved Thanksgiving
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: This is more of a true story than it appears. Franklin Roosevelt changed Thanksgiving from the last Thursday in November to the next-to-the-last Thursday, in order to give retailers a longer Christmas shopping season. It was only in December of 1941 that congress set the date of Thanksgiving to the fourth Thursday in November, which can occur as early as the 22nd or as late as November 28th.

item.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

item.title: A Unique Piece of Amber
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Amber is hardened and fossilized tree resin. When resin (which is different from sap) falls on an animal, usually an insect, that body is preserved as is. That allows us to see prehistoric bugs as they appeared in life, with its original form preserved even if it is dessicated, encased in nature's glass.This cricket encased in amber is a rare specimen, because it has a tiny gas bubble still in its abdomen. The bubble was most likely formed by chemical and bacterial action on whatever the cricket last ate, and it might be methane. In other words, it's a fart. It couldn't be expelled because resin is pretty thick before it turns to stone, and the cricket was dead anyway. But this bubble still moves when you turn the amber! That requires liquid, and with a little digging I found out that amber can contain water despite the resin's dehydrating properties under certain conditions. Cool. (via Geeks Are Sexy)

item.title: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
item.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
item.content:encoded: The first time I played was during a hurricane. It was late 1999, I was 10 years old, Hurricane Irene was bearing down on Miami, and my friend Ryan had come over to spend the night. He had brought his copy of , the game a year old at that point, and his plan was that we should play it all the way to the end. This was a bold goal for two idiot preteen boys, and though we plowed through the entire Child Link part of the game and the start of Adult Link's quest to release the temple sages, the Water Temple claimed us as its own. We didn't have a Prima strategy guide or the internet to help us out, so after hours (and I do mean hours) of raising and lowering water levels, we gave up. I didn't end up beating my own copy of , which my dad bought for me as soon as the hurricane passed, until the next summer in Venezuela, but even then, even as an idiot preteen boy, I knew I had played something special.Twenty-seven years later, I am playing something special again. Well, I am playing the same thing, but newer, fresher, and more beautiful. I am playing the remake of , and I have loved every second of it so far. As a remake, this is a work of art. The graphics are gorgeous, if a bit shiny. The story is as good as it ever was, only now with a lot more voice acting that gives characters personality. The gameplay is much the same, albeit with some quality-of-life changes; the ability to swap equipped items with one button is a huge upgrade to pausing and going into the menu every three seconds. I'm not saying that the remake is now the best way to play —there's something to be said for the friction that came with the original's technical limitations—but I saying that the remake justifies its own existence with an attention to detail and a commitment to thrilling gameplay that shines through in every second of playtime. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T4Eh0M-Sh_g

item.title: Closing The Sandwich Shop
item.author: Ernie Smith
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.content:encoded: As another media-industry stalwart shuts down, it remains essential for media outlets to control their own destinies.takes over the stock market, it’s more than a little weird to write a little lament to the way the internet once was.But we recently lost , one of the few news sites that’s been here more or less the entire time. And the reason cited sounds quite familiar:The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable.I’m sure that’s certainly true. But I also know that Salon has likely hit more of those road bumps than most. When it started, it was a site build around news, yes, but also a robust comments section. Then it gave that up, willingly. As I wrote in an aside earlier this year:A testament to its legacy: used the software as the anchor of its digital community for more than 15 years, only shutting it down in 2011 out of concerns it wasn’t where the Web was going. With another 15 years of retrospect, can we argue that this was probably a bad move? Perhaps.I don’t want to argue prescience, but I do think decisions like these, where we handed off the infrastructure of our own destines to other companies in hopes that maybe they’d have a better idea than we would? They ultimately cost us necessary momentum and foundational strength.The thing is, media outlets like , which got its initial seed funding from Apple and Adobe (and Adobe continued to financially support for years after its launch), have long been swimming upstream. It had to ride a series of technology trends (search, social, video) to stay afloat. It wasn’t like had originated any of these; it had to survive on the back of a tech ecosystem that saw financial opportunity in journalism, but not enough to build around it forever.(It’s not like Adobe has invested millions of dollars in Salon anytime recently, after all. Free idea, Adobe: Maybe do that. Would be a great goodwill opportunity, considering the creatives you’ve frustrated of late.)Matt Wolfbridge, the editor of the great which I’ve contributed to in the past, wrote a loving, but honest, take about where went. He arrived there after its initial heyday, the period that gave us Joan Walsh and later Glenn Greenwald. While he was there, he grew its social presence in a big way. He didn’t hide its flaws, but he did note how much he loved the thing:Everyone was happy for me when I did leave for a surging news startup, which I did with a degree of sadness. was the first thing in my professional life that had ever gone right. And it was staffed by many brilliant people whose devotion to the written word was so great they put up with the ownership’s demands. I am grateful for the time I spent there.I didn’t work at . I can’t claim any sort of institutional knowledge of what was there, like Matt can. But what I can say is that stuff like this makes me endlessly sad.’s late-stage owner: A reflection of 31 years of pivots?, in its own way, has reflected all the good and bad trends of digital-first journalism over the past 31 years. The most recent trend it reflected? The weird owner nobody who ever of, taking it over, Bending Spoons-style.That’s right, went down the same road that another great site in the internet’s digital legacy, , did. It, too, was sold to a company based in Malta, with a background in iGaming, the shorthand term for “online gambling.” , whatever its qualities before this shutdown happened, stuck out like a sore thumb in the context of Find.co’s product catalog.“Leading Performance Marketing in Crypto” is not something one would associate with a long-running publication. But when I read “company that has crypto and iGaming interests buys website with 31 years of SEO juice,” I think to myself, “Oh, they want the Google ranking, not the outlet.”I could be wrong. Maybe the Find.co folks are perfectly nice people who thought it’d be fun to make a bet on traditional journalism at a time when it seems like nobody else was.But given the way that media brands get put through the wringer by both internal and external technology partners, it’s not hard to look at situations like these with a raised eyebrow. After all, today it’s . Tomorrow, it could be another legendary site. The problem with building empires on the shared infrastructure of others is that they’re changing the infrastructure even if you don’t want them to. You’re forced to react to it at all times.And sometimes, those companies don’t even know what the hell they’re doing, either. I’ve been following the recent SEO-website headlines with great interest after it came out that Google’s AI Mode, a search feature that the company heavily pushed onto its search engine, was less profitable than the old version of Google. And that has led Google to test minimizing it in searches. (Unfortunately, that doesn’t include the much-maligned AI overviews, but hey, at least &udm=14 exists.)That’s telling. Like the infamous Facebook-driven pivot to video that was based on inflated data, an entire industry has been forced to leap based on bets that another company is making without knowing that what they’re doing is actually working.What a legendary Wawa can teach you about top-down decision-makingRecently, I was on the home page of , a paper where I once helped start a free daily newspaper, reading about how a community was protesting in an attempt to save a beloved Wawa location. The story I think offers a neat parallel for the challenges journalism faces. This location meant a lot to the students of William & Mary, but Wawa wants more stores with attached gas stations. Classic example of making a 30,000-foot decision without looking at what’s happening on the ground.The tech industry is full of decisions like these, where bold bets are made at a high level without understanding where the value equation actually lies. Our latest initiative requires us to strategically pivot towards gas stations, so we must stop serving 19-year-olds who want a hoagie in the middle of the night. We need to push people towards AI so we keep them on site longer, so we hurt all the symbiotic relationships we created over the past 30 years.At the bottom of the article, my eye was drawn to the fine print, presumably put there by the Tribune bosses:The use of any content on this website for the purpose of training artificial intelligence systems, algorithms, machine learning models, text and data mining, or similar use is strictly prohibited without explicit written consent.We are now past the point where media outlets are going to be nice about it. They’ve been burned way too many times. This top-down stuff is gonna cost us everything we actually care about if we don’t stop it. Lowell “The Hammer” Stanley is as close as you’ll find to a real-life Saul Goodman. Which is why it’s shocking to learn that, like Goodman infamously once did, Stanley just had his law license suspended.Just wanted to offer a quick shout to zsKnight, the developer of ZSNES, who has made an utterly charming game collection called Retro Endurance 8 Bit. The gimmick: The game keeps changing, channel-clicker style, as you rush through levels. (Think /, but with a quirky sense of humor all its own.) Find it on Steam here.Solidarity with the William & Mary students trying to save their Wawa. Find this one an interesting read? Share it with a pal!

item.title: To Catch a Ransomware Scammer, FBI Posed as Both Victim and Attacker
item.author: Mikael Thalen
item.content:encoded: Federal prosecutors say the FBI posed as both a ransomware victim and threat actor during an undercover operation targeting a Florida-based company.The company, run by defendant Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar and an unnamed business associate, began in 2020 and claimed to offer data recovery services for victims of ransomware. An filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island on Wednesday alleges that Palacio’s business, listed as “Company A,” purported to have "advanced cryptographic tools" that could be used to "restore 100%" of a victim's data. Yet prosecutors say Palacio, charged with three counts of wire fraud, had no such capabilities and instead secretly negotiated with the ransomware gangs to obtain the decryption keys himself. Palacio, the indictment adds, would then bill clients for an amount greater than what the ransomware gangs charged in order to turn a profit."It was part of the scheme and artifice to defraud that PALACIO used Company A to intentionally misrepresent to companies in the United States who were victims of ransomware attacks that Company A could help them decrypt and recover their files without paying a ransom," the indictment says.As part of the investigation into the company, an undercover FBI agent in June posed as a representative for a fictitious Rhode Island-based business that alleged it had fallen victim to a ransomware attack.Another FBI employee posed as a member of a ransomware gang and encrypted several files on a computer operated by the fictitious company. The federal employee also left a ransom note on the computer with contact information.The fictitious business then contacted Palacio's company and held an initial meeting on June 8 in which an agent said it did not want to pay the ransom. Palacio during subsequent discussions charged the fictitious company $2,750 to conduct an initial forensic assessment.After offering the undercover FBI agent a contract outlining his company's services, Palacio on June 14 contacted the federal employee posing as the ransomware threat actor over email. Palacio requested the "lowest possible price for the decryptor," the indictment says, before accepting a 0.2 bitcoin offer, worth roughly $13,000 at the time. On June 16, Palacio's business associate reached out to the fictitious FBI-run business posing as the victim, and said the files could be decrypted for $13,260, which the FBI paid. The following day, Palacio once again contacted the fake ransomware operator, which the FBI was also running, and asked to reduce the payment from $13,000 to $4,000 in an attempt to increase the company’s profit.The FBI employee, posing as the ransomware threat actor, counter-offered with $6,000. On June 19, Palacio paid the FBI employee 0.0948 bitcoin, worth $6,003 at the time. Five days later, the undercover FBI agent gave Palacio the decryption key. In total, according to the indictment, Palacio's company netted $10,010 in profit as part of the FBI sting. Numerous legitimate companies are also listed as victims in the indictment, including a Kansas-based business that Palacio allegedly charged $720,000. In that case, prosecutors say Palacio kept all remaining funds after paying a ransomware gang approximately $445,000 in bitcoin for the decryption key.If convicted, Palacio would be required to forfeit any proceeds and property obtained through the company’s alleged fraud.The case against Palacio is not the first time the FBI has targeted individuals in the ransomware recovery space. In April, a Florida man who previously worked at a cyber incident response company to conspiring to commit ransomware attacks against U.S. companies. The man, according to the DOJ, abused his role at the company to provide the BlackCat ransomware gang with “confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his company’s clients” in order to maximize ransom payments.

item.title: The Katseye Concussion Saga Raises The Question Of Who’s In Charge In K-Pop
item.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
item.content:encoded: Last week, I couldn’t stop watching videos of Katseye's performance in Austin, Texas, where three members of the group writhed on stage while a fourth, Megan Skiendiel—who had recently suffered a concussion—wore protective sunglasses and was propped up on a stool to the side. She sat with her legs crossed, expressionless, as if she were not on stage under flashing lights but instead waiting for her name to be called at the DMV. Mere feet away, her comrades in ass-shaking executed their choreography with their usual precision.Skiendiel’s presence on stage adds so little to the performance that you wonder why she’s even there. Every once in a while, she raised her mic to sing her part in a song, devoid of any expression or movement. The dissonance of the scene was so absurd that it generated memesofitsown, and even fan art; this week, Skiendiel posted backstage photos of herself in her sunglasses, with the caption “Cuntcussion.” https://www.instagram.com/p/Dfy7Ix7G0Ia/?img_index=1

item.title: Cornyn Nixes Judgeship for OLC Head After Shouting Match With Ted Cruz
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Author of Boat Strike Memo Is From OhioOutgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) appears to have killed the judicial nomination of T. Elliot Gaiser, the 37-year-old head of the Office of Legal Counsel at the Trump DOJ who authored legal justifications for some of the administration’s most egregious extralegal conduct, including the lawless boat strike campaign.“He’s not from Texas. He hasn’t been vetted. And this is a lifetime job, and there’s better qualified people to hold that job,” Cornyn told the AP. “This is part, of course, of the constitutional responsibility of senators in the Senate to provide advice and consent. But it’s hard to provide advice and consent when there’s zero consultation, which happened in that case.”Gaiser did not appear on the confirmation hearing yesterday for a batch of Trump judicial nominees (who as a group refused to say that the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021). Cornyn’s leverage over the nomination comes from the Senate’s “blue-slip” tradition, still honored by Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Charles Grassley (R-IA), of not moving judicial nominations without the approval of home state senators.Cornyn’s public break with the administration came after he and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) got into a loud argument on the Senate floor Tuesday over the Gaiser nomination. The whole imbroglio is heavily colored by Cornyn losing re-election in the GOP primary after Trump endorsed his opponent Ken Paxton, who went on to lose the general election that Cornyn his convinced he himself would have won.Things continued to spill out in public on Wednesday with the Justice Department tacking a whack at Cornyn: “It is deeply disappointing that Senator Cornyn would choose political obstruction over advancing a highly qualified nominee.”Cruz put out his own statement warning that there’s not time to confirm anyone else to the vacant judgeship: “If the Senate Judiciary Committee does not move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay the price because it will effectively give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity,” Cruz said. “That would be a tragedy.”Another outgoing GOP senator primaried by President Trump got a measure of revenge.Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), the chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, abruptly cancelled a committee vote on the nomination of Jim O’Neill to lead the National Science Foundation.O’Neill previously worked in multiple roles at the Department of Health and Human Services under Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from Secretary Kennedy,” said Cassidy, who indicated that some other members of the committee shared his concerns.Cassidy’s move effectively scuttled the nomination.Election 2026 By the NumbersA few new data points as the vote-counting nears an end:Democrats lead in the national House vote has expanded to 14-percentage points, the largest margin by either party since Democrats romped by 16.6 points in the 1974 post-Watergate election.Democrats have won at least 257 House seats, with six races still uncalled by the AP.At least 109 House seats will be held by freshman, the most since at least 1998.: Allies have launched Team Pete PAC to back another presidential run by the former secretary of transportation. (Politico): The Democratic senator from Arizona is bringing longtime aide Emma Brown back into the fold as he considers a White House run. (Politico): “Looking at it right now, it’s absolutely a savagely brutal map,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH), the incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. (Politico)The Dog That’s Obviously Not BarkingAfter the Trump DOJ brought a flurry of noncitizen voting cases right before the election — touting them with press releases, press conferences, and mug shots — it has brought only one new noncitizen voting case since the Nov. 3 election, the WaPo reports.The Corruption: IRS EditionProPublica reports on under-the-radar Trump administration settlement of a claims against the IRS for leaking taxpayer info.It recalls Trump’s own settlement with the IRS and the planned creation of $1.776 billion slush fund.But it’s not Trump this time.It’s the longtime golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley.And despite the settlement, the case isn’t over yet.Two other people connected to Trump properties are trying to get in on the action: a retired accountant at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley and a former lifeguard at the Trump golf club in Westchester County, New York.Colorado Pubic Radio: In a new contempt of court ruling, U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney excoriated ICE for repeatedly violating court orders with its policy of immediately re-detaining immigrants after they had been ordered to be released from detention. But Sweeney declined to take any further action, ruling that ICE officials had cured the contempt of court by ceasing the practice at issue.Greg Sargent: ICE has $91 billion of no-strings-attached funding to spend on deportations between now and the end of Trump’s second term.Nicholas Kristof: Trump ‘Disappeared’ Them in 2025. I Found Them, Locked Up and Famished.Bo French Booted From Country ClubRepublican Bo French’s racist (and losing) campaign for Texas Railroad Commission has cost him his membership in the River Crest Country Club in Fort Worth. The country club’s board of directors booted him after he refused to resign his membership.Thanks For All the AI Feedback!I received quite a rich and varied response to my question yesterday about which AI tools you’ve found to be useful. Many thanks for taking the time to email.First off, y’all are awesome. You’re a remarkable cross section of creatives and what we now call “knowledge workers” (I hate that term): scientists, engineers, teachers, musicians, writers, attorneys, CEOs, founders, environmental consultants, and IT experts — many of whom are also doing side gigs for fun. Those of you who purport to be retired are busy af, serving on boards and volunteering and running your own pet projects.You’ve discovered uses for AI that range from the practical to the whimsical to the sublime. This initial sampling of reader responses are personal and side projects uses that delighted me:TPM Reader : “I manage my own forested acreage in Washington State for enjoyment, health, and minor income. I was kind of at a point where I wanted to get more focused, more deliberate, and more comprehensive in my management planning and use of my time and labor. My son suggested I get a monthly ChatGPT account to facilitate that. The results have been dazzling.”TPM Reader : “It helped me build two ten foot bird feeder poles with offset arms to stop raccoons and squirrels.”TPM Reader : “Because of ChatGPT I have been able to do a pet project, a searchable index of historic cookbooks in the public domain.”

item.title: Shh! Don’t wake Preznit Fuckwit — international geopolitics makes him sleepy
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: That’s right, the narcoleptic old fart factory’s brain went again yesterday, right in the middle of an APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in China.But before we get to that —This is just so fucking bizarre. Are we all on crazy pills right now?How creepy is this? Why is she there? She has no legitimate function in that room. How does this keep happening, in meeting after meeting? Does she simply invite herself along, and no one says ? Imagine you’re a world leader, sitting across the table from all that. How could you even concentrate, with that spectacle going on? What do you say to your spouse when you get home? ‘You will never fucking believe what happened today. The silly dipshit brought a dateYou know what? Let’s skip over the question of why is Natty there, because here’s a better question: Why is there? What value does presence add? All he does is ramble incoherently about his own imaginary accomplishments, and piss and moan if he doesn’t get a toy.“There’s never been a time like this. But of course it was— right here— in this [unintelligible] palace that President— Quezon bestowed General Douglas MacArthur with a gold— baton, and the rank of Field Marshall in the Philippine Army. I’d like to have you do that for me, if you don’t mind. I’d love that. I mean, why the hell shouldn’t I get that?”Yeah, come on, President Marcos, get with the program. Don’t you know by now that Donny always gets a participation trophy, no matter where he goes? FIFA gave him one. So did NASA. So give the whiny little piss-baby his fucking gold baton before he falls to pieces, like a child in a supermarket who can’t have candy.Seriously, what’s the point of even having Donny there at your meeting? My advice to every international organization — APEC, the Quad, NATO, the G7, the United Nations, the OAS, — is this: the next time you hold a wingding, don’t bother inviting Donny. I promise that you won’t even notice his absence, except for maybe air quality having been improved by the lack of narcoleptic farts. After Dear Leader shit the bed in the Philippines, it was on to China, where Donny was serenely unaware that he was the mark.“They’re treating me extremely well for China, and I have a lot of respect and a good relationship with President Xi ... nobody is gonna play games with us.”Oh my god, this gullible goofus has no idea he was being set up to be swindled. He’s so easily manipulated that it isn’t even funny. the Chinese are treating him ‘extremely well’ — they’re buttering him up so they can pick his pockets. Donny is like the chump at the blackjack table in a Las Vegas casino. He’s losing his shirt, but all he can do is marvel over how they keep giving him free drinks. Donny: Fox bobblehead: “Are you going to tell them to stop buying Iranian oil?”Donny: “You know, when they say that China is working with— with uh, Iran, or Russia’s working with Iran, no, no. What, they’re giving some information? We have all the information that they give. We know exactly what they’re giving. It’s peanuts.”Hang on, did Dear Leader just hand-wave away China and Russia feeding intel to Iran, because ? He did, didn’t he. What in the actual fuck?Look, it’s not just that’s being provided to Iran. China is Iran’s largest buyer of crude oil. Russia is helping Iran re-arm itself. Do you imagine that Donny doesn’t know that, or just doesn’t care, because — as he so idiotically puts it — I can’t decide which scenario is worse. What a great idea it was, to let a greedy and easily-flattered shit-for-brains be president. Tell me, is allowing our adversaries to get away with aiding a country we’re at war with, because you expect you’ll personally benefit from doing so — would that be a I’m hopeful that we’ll find out at Donny’s third impeachment trial, next year.Now I can hear you out there, going ‘but Uncle Jeff, what about the Nodfather? You promised at the top of this post that Donny would be sleeping.’Yes, I know I did, but we had to get through the boring-but-more-important stuff first. Don’t make me come over there and explain how clickbait works.Holy fuck, Dear Leader is out like a light. He doesn’t move a millimeter during the entire clip. The only way to tell that you’re not looking at a still photograph is that you can see Soybean Scott Bessent’s smug haughty head moving in the background, behind Donny.Who thought it would be a good idea to let a doddering demento attend four meetings across two countries in one day? I have an idea. Can we get that Arlington Guard back in here, to stand behind Donny and scream ‘ALL PRESIDENTS WILL MAINTAIN AN ATMOSPHERE OF NOT FALLING THE FUCK ASLEEP AND EMBARRASSING YOUR ENTIRE COUNTRY’?Because that would fucking rule.And now, on to our Daily Claudia.Here are two photos taken in Plymouth, MA, back in the early 1990s, by Daughter Katie. This first one is from before she was old enough to have figured out that whole ‘don’t crop people’s heads off’ thing.And this second one, thankfully, is from after.Have a great Thursday, everyone. Oh wait — one final thing before I let you go.I have no idea what this unsubscriber means by ‘too much porn type stuff.’ Is it the cussing? Folks, I hope you’re all reading these posts and discovering that I have a sweary fucking mouth you plunk down your hard-earned cash on a paid subscription. Oh, and don’t be fooled by all the free drinks at the blackjack table.Okay, you can all fucking well have a great fucking Thursday.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: The NFL Trade Deadline Is Fine Right Where It Is

item.content:encoded: If you were up early last Sunday, you may have borne witness to this NFL season’s most catastrophic play, in which Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson took out Pats QB Drake Maye for the season, and then took out for the season mere seconds later. ACH!Not only did these two injuries severely hamper the postseason prospects of both the Patriots and Lions, but they also turned what would have otherwise been a compelling Munich game into a big ol’ doo-doo fest. Even worse, both Detroit and New England suffered these losses the NFL’s trade deadline had already passed. If the Pats want help at QB, they’re gonna have to make nice with Handsome Jimmy Garoppolo, or grab some other slob off the free-agent wire. The plight of both these teams has a few pundits wondering if the league should move the trade deadline to even later in the regular season, to which Arif Hasan and I say: Fuck that. item.title: High-End Furniture Marketplace AptDeco Is Taking People’s Furniture and Not Paying Them
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: This article has been updated with comment from AptDeco.Last month, Erin sold a $3,000 large designer table on AptDeco, a white glove high-end furniture marketplace. More than a month later, she feels like she’s been literally robbed.“AptDeco sent three men to physically collect my table on October 13, and here we are on November 16, with no payment and no concrete explanation for where my $2,000 (after their absurd $900 fee) is,” Erin told me. “It genuinely feels like I’ve had something stolen from me.”AptDeco is a Y Combinator-backed company whose entire purpose is to take the risk out of places like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist for designer furniture resale. It advertises itself as “simple and seamless,” and says “we handle pickup, delivery, and payments,” and claims that it pays sellers “within 5-10 business days.” But over the last few months, people who have sold furniture on the platform say that AptDeco has sold their furniture and taken it from their houses, but hasn’t paid them. 404 Media agreed to only use Erin’s first name because she is still trying to get her money from the company.“Adding to the chorus of people who sold an item thru AptDeco and never received payment. I have no idea what to do at this point,” another says. “Can we do a class action lawsuit?” another reads.“They owed me money since September 30th,” a fourth says. Every recent review and complaint on AptDeco’s Better Business Bureau page is from sellers who have not been paid: “Almost 6 weeks after they picked up and not being paid Pick up was a nightmare too No calls nobody doing anything Do NOT SELL ON APTDECO,” one reads. Another states “I have been in an endless loop with customer service for 2 months trying to get my payout for the bed I sold. I am losing faith that I will ever see this money. Extremely frustrated at this experience.”On AptDeco’s website, everything appears to be business as usual. You can still buy and sell furniture, and there is no indication of anything wrong at all. 404 Media’s repeated attempts to reach AptDeco to ask what was going on went unreturned.In communications with sellers seen by 404 Media, AptDeco’s customer service representatives have repeatedly blamed their payment processor, a “technical bug,” or have said the payment is “moving through the system.” On November 3, AptDeco told Erin that a bug had prevented her from being paid, that the payment team “retried” it, and that she would be paid within 10 days. “I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally, so you should see it in your bank account by then - hopefully sooner! At this point, we’re doing everything we can to get your payout processed,” a customer support email reviewed by 404 Media reads. On Tuesday, two weeks after the company told her the payment had been retried, a different customer service representative followed up and said “I'm truly sorry — I know this isn't the update you were hoping for. Your payout is still being prioritized by our payments team, and I want to be honest with you: I don't yet have a confirmed release date or timeline to share.”Several other people who have sold items on AptDeco recently told 404 Media they’re experiencing the same problem.Harry Heymann sold a Room & Board couch on AptDeco in late September and still has not been paid the $120 he is owed by the platform. The messages he’s gotten from AptDeco customer support read much the same as Erin’s: They claim “a technical bug on our end held up your payout” and the customer service representative said “I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally.” Late last week, he got what reads like an AI-generated message that reads “I know how frustrating this has been. You've been waiting on your $120 payout, the date you were given has passed, and you've had to follow up to get answers. That's not the experience we want for you, and I'm truly sorry. Your case has been escalated to me, and l'm happy to be your point of contact from here. Unfortunately, the issue with our payment processor has not yet been resolved, and our team is still working on it.” Natalie Simmons sold an armoire in late August and told 404 Media she initially had a good experience compared to using other platforms. But then she never got her money. “After so many uncomfortable situations on different social sites I was so happy when I found AptDeco,” she told me. “I received notification that my payment would arrive in 3-5 business days through the portal in app. That was Aug 30th. I tried calling but the voicemail says leave a message and they will respond by email. I emailed several times and finally after 2 weeks and a few voicemails I received an email that there was a glitch with their payment system and I will receive payment within 5-10 business days. After another 2 weeks I called and emailed again that I still didn’t receive payment. They sent another email with the exact same story. I just want to get paid. It’s not even that much but it’s the principle.”It’s not just sellers who have had issues with the platform. One customer, K Turner, bought a couch and tried to return it. Rather than giving her a refund, the company said they would relist it at the price she paid and then give her a “refund” of whatever it sold for minus fees. The couch resold quickly at the beginning of September and the company told her she would quickly get her “refund.” More than a month later, on October 20, they told her “I have gone ahead and processed that refund ($600) manually. Please allow 5-10 business days for this refund to be reflected back to your original form of payment.” She has still not gotten her money. “The communication was decent at first, but once they confirmed the item resold on September 8th, they then went silent. It took me a month to finally get a response. They confirmed that the item resold at the full listing price of $600 and that I would receive my refund to my original payment in 5 - 10 business days,” Turner told me. “That was nearly a month ago, and I still don't have my money. So, they effectively double-dipped. They got my money from the original order and then collected money by reselling it. And who knows if they ever gave the money to the original seller; maybe they triple-dipped. I have threatened legal action twice now.”The customers I spoke to have no idea what happens next. Some of them said they were going to file claims in small claims court or are considering a class action lawsuit. But the company is mostly giving them what appear to be canned, copy-pasted statements that come from a revolving cast of customer support email addresses, and no actual updates. Four emails from 404 Media asking for comment, including emails sent to the company’s CEO, have not been returned. AptDeco promises a high-end, safe experience when compared to somewhere like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist, and markets itself primarily for more expensive, lightly-used furniture. The people I spoke to said they wish they had just stayed off the platform altogether.“The irony is that I’m now feeling safer selling expensive designer furniture directly to strangers on Facebook Marketplace than through a platform whose entire purpose is supposedly to make these transactions safer and more secure,” Erin said. “At this point, AptDeco has my furniture, I have no money, and I’m left chasing them for something I’m already owed. It’s an incredibly unsettling position to be in, particularly when so many other sellers seem to be experiencing the same thing. The fact that I continue to receive email marketing newsletters and see them selling via Google Ads—paying that platform before their sellers—is infuriating.”After this article was published (and three days after we initially asked for comment), an AptDeco spokesperson gave 404 Media a convoluted explanation involving “bot swarms,” which it blamed for the delays in seller payouts. “Over the past few months, we’ve been dealing with an unprecedented volume of bot activity, some of it malicious. This has created a myriad of challenges that we’ve been actively working to address.These bot swarms, along with the broader cybersecurity challenges of an AI-evolving world, prompted us to significantly strengthen our site’s security to ensure the long-term protection of our buyers and sellers,” the spokesperson said. “To be clear, customer data has not been compromised in any way. However, we’ve been investing heavily in preventative measures to further protect our community. Unfortunately, some of these efforts have resulted in delays in seller payouts. As you can imagine, cybersecurity is a complex and sensitive topic, making it challenging to communicate all the details broadly. That said, the issue has now been resolved, and outstanding payouts are being processed. Any seller with questions can email and will hear back within 1 business day. We appreciate your patience and understanding.”When I asked for clarification because it was not clear how bot swarms would affect payouts, the spokesperson said “the bot swarm did not affect seller payouts.”“We deployed code to further improve protections for our customers (given the bot swarms) which inadvertently impacted seller payout processing. Providing additional technical context would require a detailed understanding of our codebase and would likely be more information than is relevant or useful to readers,” they added. “That said, we sincerely apologize to our customers for the delays and are committed to making things right. The issue has been resolved, our security infrastructure remains extremely robust, and outstanding payouts are being processed. We appreciate you reaching out and giving us the opportunity to clarify. This will be our final comment on the matter.”also pointed out that the company is being sued by American Express for allegedly failing to pay a $158,461 credit card bill from 2024; that case is in default judgment but is ongoing.

item.title: The Energy Tax of Living in a New Place
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Before moving abroad, I was really independent. I loved socialising, visiting new places, trying new things. But over the past few years I’ve become so much more anxious and reserved, and I only just realised why.When you live somewhere familiar, life is second nature. You know the language, the systems, the culture, and the social expectations. You have routines, support and things are predictable.But when you live abroad, the energy required to participate in life increases. Socialising, going to appointments, buying a coffee, answering the phone. Everything requires so much more planning, energy and courage.When you’re already mentally exhausted, you have less energy for the things you want and should do. You avoid situations that feel difficult. You become more reserved, less confident, more isolated and less independent.I’m writing this at the airport after spending 2.5 months in Tokyo and feeling the above . I’ve never been what you’d call outgoing, but after the initial rush of being here wore off after a few weeks, I definitely noticed myself becoming “more reserved, less confident, more isolated and less independent”. Some days, I barely left my apartment because I couldn’t bear summoning the energy to make a plan, negotiate a new restaurant, or figure out how to get from point A to point B on the train. I sought out places that were easy: online ticketing, digital ordering screens, English menus, chain stores & restaurants.The confidence piece is probably the hardest for me. I have to work hard in social situations with people I don’t know, and doing that in a language I don’t speak and in a cultural context I don’t fully understand is challenging, especially when I need to do it 10 times a day. I rely on humor in situations like these and, well, I don’t know how to be funny in Japan. Confidence tends to be a pervasive trait — a dip in one area of your life causes an overall decline across many areas. And all this is coming after living for the past decade in a place where I never felt like I fit in.Anyway, it’s been eye-opening, this shift in energy & confidence. I’m onto the next place soon, but this is something I definitely need to keep an eye on.

item.title: How Much Better Can Matthew Schaefer Get?
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: Matthew Schaefer, the best NHL defenseman of the next generation and maybe already this one, is a pleasure to watch. The first unanimous Calder winner in 33 years, he finished second on the New York Islanders in both goals and assists last season. As a defenseman! As an 18-year-old! There is a damn teenager at the controls of the Isles' offense, driving play at both ends of the ice and looking so impossibly assured that he was named alternate captain in his second year, and nobody thinks this is weird or fluky. Sure, he was a no-brainer for first overall pick, but even wunderteens usually require some period of adjustment.Year two has started even hotter. Twenty games in, Schaefer leads the Islanders in points (nine goals, 15 assists), all the while playing the fourth-most minutes per game of the entire league. Young legs are nice to have, but he's out here playing entire overtimes without coming off. His defense is good, if not quite elite—he's still vulnerable to being forechecked, and his positioning can sometimes be off—but the stage for the Schaefer Show is 200 feet long. He's a demon in transition and a menace in the offensive zone. "We're watching greatness kind of evolve," teammate Mathew Barzal said.The most complimentary thing I can say about Schaefer's scoring is that he is not by any means a chucker. He's not perched at the blue line, clapping pucks on a prayer, like some empty-calorie offensive defensemen I could name. His very reasonable shot percentage both last year and this represent neither a player who has been especially lucky, nor a volume scorer taking away other, potentially shorter-odds opportunities. He is earning his points with his decisions.

item.title: Black Neighborhoods Are Twice as Likely To House a Data Center, Study Finds
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: Developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods, according to a new study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University.According to the study, “Redlining in the Age of AI: The Relationship between Data Center Locations and Race in the US” majority-Black neighborhoods have 2.2 times the odds of hosting a data center than a white neighborhood in the same state. The number goes up to 2.6 in majority-Hispanic neighborhoods and 4.2 times in majority-Asian neighborhoods. “As the share of Black, Hispanic, and Asian residents in a neighborhood increases, so do the odds that the neighborhood hosts a data center,” the researchers wrote.The researchers ran the numbers by examining 81,000 US census tracts and location data for 5,291 data centers. “We found that these racial disparities persist even after accounting for factors such as population, household income, education, land costs, proximity to major transmission lines, and state fixed effects,” they wrote. “These results hold even though data centers are concentrated in and around metropolitan areas, which are often more racially diverse.”“We really wanted to look at this on a nationwide scale to see: is this something that fits into this broader structural racism story?” CSINT executive director Samantha Bradshaw told 404 Media. “What we did find was yes [...] neighborhoods that have data centers tend to have a higher ratio of people of color.”Bradshaw and co-author Dhanaraj Thakur told 404 Media that they were inspired to do the study after reading stories about data centers in Memphis, Tennessee polluting Black and Brown communities. Another high profile case occurred in Taylor, Texas where a white family donated a tract of land to the city with the intention it become a public part. That land abutted a Black neighborhood. The city never built a park there and now it’s slated to become a data centerAccording to the researchers, the historical legacy of — the process of denying Americans of color loans and other opportunities to keep them in specific neighborhoods — is to blame for some of this. Data centers are often built near transmission lines because they provide ease of access to power infrastructure, for example. Those transmission lines were often built in majority Black neighborhoods in America. Thakur said he doubted that data centers developers were seeking to intentionally put data centers in communities of color. “It’s just how embedded race is with all these other factors,” he said. The study distinguished between several different kinds of data centers and noted there are massive differences between hyperscalers like what Meta, Google, and Grok are building and smaller mixed use buildings that often serve as network transmission hubs as well as compute warehouses, which the study called “co-location facilities.” When a hyperscaler comes to town, the developers sometimes promise economic investment in the community where it’s being constructed and those facilities typically aren’t built in communities of color..Meta is building a $50 billion data center in rural Louisiana. Community leaders there have said it would bring 1,000 permanent jobs and that sales tax revenues have already jumped 2,000 percent, leading to a $50,000 bonus for area teachers. Even here, there is disparity. Most of the hyperscalers that promise massive economic benefits to local communities are built in white rural communities. The study makes several suggestions about what to do about all this including data center-specific zoning regulations, prioritizing racial equity in discussions around building them, and requiring racial impact statements for data centers before they’re built. Thakur and Bradshaw emphasized that tech policy should be a negotiation between the companies that provide the tech and the communities that use it. Data centers have spurred these conversations — they’re physical representations of Big Tech’s powers, a power that Americans recently rejected at the ballot box. “AI has a physical geography, and that geography is shaped by political and social history,” the researchers wrote in the study.“I think the issue around how racial justice, civil rights plays into many other kinds of policies —health, education, housing, whatever it is — we just don't see enough of that consideration in tech policy, and I think this this kind of analysis shows why this that why we should be doing that, thinking about that more,” Thakur said.Bradshaw agreed. “If you look at who's represented in tech policy and who built these systems, who designs them, who engineers them, it's a very specific kind of white male Silicon Valley California ideology engineer, and that is not representative of the technology and its users,” she said. “So I think bringing in these perspectives is really really important because then we can truly think about ways to design a tech future that is for everybody.

item.title: Mass Surveillance and GTA
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: I got an internal ICE document that shows the agency is paying telecommunications giant AT&T for access to raw data. Multiple experts I showed the document to say this is a continuation of Hemisphere, a thought-to-be-shuttered mass surveillance program, but which they say is now back, just in direct payments from ICE to AT&T. “The Biden administration shut down Hemisphere after I and Rep. Biggs repeatedly questioned this warrantless mass phone surveillance program. 404 Media’s reporting shows that the Trump-Vance administration has created a zombie version of Hemisphere surveillance, and given it to their chosen enforcers at ICE,” Senator Ron Wyden said in a statement.Also, happy Grand Theft Auto day! We hope you play and contribute less to the world’s economy.Immigration and Customs Enforcement is paying telecommunications giant AT&T millions of dollars to have AT&T’s analysts sift through mountains of raw AT&T data for a wide variety of investigations, according to an internal ICE document obtained by 404 Media, other procurement records, and experts who reviewed those records. Civil liberty experts havecalled it a mass surveillance program, and they say the data can include trillions of phone records and location data. The AT&T product, interchangeably called Data Analytics and Support Services or Data Analytical Services, appears to be related to an earlier surveillance program called Hemisphere, in which AT&T provided U.S. authorities at state, local, and federal levels access to AT&T user data. Though that program shut down, ICE is still paying for access to raw data under this new arrangement with AT&T, according to the restricted ICE procurement document obtained by 404 Media. The program likely affects more than just AT&T customers because the company connects phone calls for other phone companies, meaning noncustomers are likely swept up too, according to a surveillance expert.“This requirement provides ICE access to AT&T’s raw data and experienced analysts,” the document obtained by 404 Media reads.AT&T told 404 Media the data is made available under a valid legal order, but experts point out it requires an administrative subpoena, which agencies can issue themselves and don’t require a judge’s approval, raising concerns that ICE can use the data for essentially whatever it wants. The document also shows how financial incentives play a part in providing data to ICE.“The Biden administration shut down Hemisphere after I and Rep. Biggs repeatedly questioned this warrantless mass phone surveillance program. 404 Media’s reporting shows that the Trump-Vance administration has created a zombie version of Hemisphere surveillance, and given it to their chosen enforcers at ICE,” Senator Ron Wyden told 404 Media in a statement.Christopher Soghoian, a surveillance expert who worked for Senator Wyden for a decade until September, told 404 Media, “It’s bad enough that AT&T is mining its customers’ private phone records as a paid service for ICE, but because AT&T is also mining the records of other wholesale telecom companies, consumers can’t vote with their wallets and switch carriers to protect their privacy.”Last September, ICE posted a procurement record a contract to AT&T for access to its Data Analytics and Support Services. When ICE announced the purchase, an attached document to the listing was marked as “controlled” and not available to the public. 404 Media subsequently obtained the document through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request with ICE.The Financial Times previously reported on the public procurement records but did not report on the restricted document at the time.This segment is a paid ad. If you’re interested in advertising, Use code 404MEDIA The way cable and local news cover Grand Theft Auto has radically changed over the years. Of course, American culture changed too. Matthew Gault wrote this illuminating piece on just that, and he watched a lot, a lot, of old news coverage of the game franchise to figure out what is different today. (It’s money.), remember when an army unit offered soldiers time off to play the new game, they agreed to more years of military service? Turns out, some people thought that was a great deal. Or at least they really wanted to play GTA at launch. 43 soldiers from the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion signed up for this program, . Sgt. Jamire Smith told the outlet “I’m all campaign. I’m all about the heist,” and “I think I have a good 24 hours to waste on it.” In exchange, Smith agreed to six more years in the Army. I don’t know if the game is good, man., meaning you can’t go into a store and just buy it. You have to download it from the digital store onto your console. The CEO of GameStop, which is obviously a company with its own stupid history too, : “Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it’s also hurt GameStop.”The Wachowski sisters are reclaiming the Matrix. The Matrix has been at the center of a lot of recent culture, or really culture wars, long after the original film and even the two earlier sequels came out. The whole exhausting red pill, black pill thing. Lilly Wachowski tried to reclaim that narrative before, by telling Elon Musk and Ivanka Trump when they invoked the red pill. Now, the Wachowskis are trying to reclaim the Matrix more literally. the pair have formally notified Warner Bros “they are exercising their copyright termination rights.” Meaning, the sisters might control the fate of the Matrix as soon as February 2029. The next new sequel is still in development. facing disruptions after the downtime of its internal classified network, from journalist Dustin Volz. “Employees at headquarters are under ‘code orange’ for Thursday day shift, meaning non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors,” he wrote.Anthropic is going public. The company raised more than $100 billion in a record setting IPO, . That valued the company at around $1.5 trillion. Maybe people saying the bubble would burst after all the Nvidia news were a little hasty.That’s the newsletter for today. Let’s see if they mention any fun criminal encryption stuff in any GTA missions.
