item.title: How homelessness and racism intersect.
item.author: SRS0=kL4K=JH=mail70.suw17.mcsv.net=bounce-mc.us19_228507186.17295061-8782042e9f@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: Homelessness Funding Is on the Line. Here’s How to Protect It.Today, the National Alliance to End Homelessness is leading a national day of action to protect federal homelessness funding (National Alliance to End Homelessness). Advocates are asking Congress to add a few lines to its next spending bill that would require the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to renew every Continuum of Care project expiring this fiscal year for 12 months, without a new competition (National Low Income Housing Coalition).The Continuum of Care program is the largest federal source of money for local homelessness work. It pays for programs like permanent supportive housing, where people get a stable home along with services like health care and job support (National Low Income Housing Coalition), and transitional housing, which gives people a safe place to stay while they look for a permanent home (National Association of Counties).The Trump administration has spent the past year trying to limit spending on homelessness. In July 2025, the president signed an executive order directing agencies to end support for Housing First policies, which give people a permanent home quickly without first requiring sobriety, treatment or a job (The White House). But Housing First has been federal policy under presidents of both parties since 2003 (Associated Press), and it has proven to be the most effective way to rehouse people (National Alliance to End Homelessness).HUD then wrote new rules for this year’s Continuum of Care grants that put the president’s order into practice. In August, a federal judge ruled that those rules were unlawful. HUD had set aside $1.3 billion of this year’s funding for new transitional housing and service-only projects, a change that would have cut money from many programs already keeping people housed (National Association of Counties). The judge also struck down rules that required programs to follow the president’s executive orders and restricted diversity efforts. But in September, an appeals court let HUD move forward while it considers the case. Under HUD’s plan, only 60 percent of funding would be protected for renewals, down from nearly 90 percent. Advocates estimate that 97,000 people who were once unhoused could lose their housing as a result (National Low Income Housing Coalition).The delays are already hurting people. In Los Angeles, providers that serve domestic violence survivors and unhoused people have cut staff and drained their reserves while HUD held up their grants (LAist). As of September, more than 1,300 renewal grant agreements across the country, about one in five, had not been fully executed. “If HUD doesn’t start to reimburse agencies quickly … we’re going to see more suffering on the street,” said Myong Kim of the Downtown Women’s Center in Los Angeles.The people impacted by these funding cuts are disproportionately people of color. Black people are 14 percent of the U.S. population but 33 percent of people experiencing homelessness. Latino people make up 27.5 percent of the unhoused population, and Native and Pacific Islander people are also overrepresented. These numbers reflect generations of policy, from redlining to exclusionary zoning to landlords and lenders who still screen people out by eviction records and criminal background (National Alliance to End Homelessness). Today, Black renters are 28 percent of renters in the places Eviction Lab tracks, but 39 percent of the people facing eviction (Eviction Lab).While funding for housing is under attack, more places are choosing punishment instead. Since the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling in Grants Pass v. Johnson, more than 350 cities and 14 states have adopted tougher laws on street homelessness (Stateline). In 2022, we spoke with Jamaal of ACT UP Philadelphia about the violence of encampment sweeps (Anti-Racism Daily). “Philly says all the time, ‘We can’t afford to house people, the housing is too expensive,’ but every time we turn around, they increase funding to the police,” he told us. I think about that line a lot, because it’s still true in so many cities.To be clear, renewing these grants won’t end homelessness on its own. We still need far more affordable homes, higher wages and an end to policies that punish people for being poor. But keeping existing programs running is the least Congress can do, and it’s within reach this month. If you have five minutes today, I encourage you to send that email. For many families, these few lines in a spending bill could decide whether they stay housed this winter.

item.title: Authoritarian Fiction is Scarier Than Post-Apocalypse Dystopias
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Grim stories about the future come in two basic models. Some are about apocalyptic disasters, like a zombie uprising, an alien invasion, or a nuclear war that wipes out most of mankind, leaving our protagonists to figure out how to survive and start all over. That would include things like Mad Max, A Boy and His Dog, The Book of Eli, and . Then there's the authoritarian dystopia, in which the population is still here, but kept under the thumb of an authoritarian government. The classic example is 1984, but it would also include Soylent Green, The Handmaid's Tale, The Hunger Games, and . These stories are actually scarier, because they could more plausibly come true. In fact, most are based at least partly on events that have already happened somewhere at some time. To sum it up, apocalyptic disasters rely heavily on fantasy, while authoritarian fiction is a warning of what could happen if we aren't diligent. PBS picks these stories apart, and shows us how we might still slide down those paths.

item.title: Trump lost the race he bet everything on
item.author: 1axbqhwmo0qcdwqoqfjj3xipe99odyaoflv15f@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Last night, Mary Peltola officially won Alaska’s Senate race. The Division of Elections updated its results to show she held an outright majority. The outcome is undeniable.With Peltola’s victory, Donald Trump lost the one fight he cared about most.For months, Trump obsessed over this race. Even as he watched Republicans get swept from coast to coast, his focus stayed fixed on Alaska.Weighed down by his historic unpopularity, his party lost Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina, Ohio and South Carolina. Even Mississippi.State after state, as the election returns came in, Trump could do nothing to stop the bleeding.Yet, as his party imploded, Trump seethed and raged about Sen. Dan Sullivan’s looming defeat in Alaska.He spread misinformation about how Alaskans vote. He lied about the results, insisting that votes cast for a different candidate belonged to the incumbent.He ordered his Justice Department to sue to block certification. When my law firm beat back that lawsuit, the DOJ came after me personally. Trump went on national television and said I should go to jail.None of these attacks changed the vote count. With each new batch of ballots, Peltola’s lead grew.Last night, the dam broke.Peltola now leads by 12,458 votes. More importantly, she has won more than half of all the votes cast in the race.There will be no ranked-choice tabulation, and no room for conspiracy theories about whose votes “really” belonged to whom.And with that, Trump’s lies collapse once and for all.Sullivan’s campaign says he won’t concede until the results are certified. The campaign insists it will “let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified.”Fortunately, election results are stubborn. The numbers are what they are. They do not require a concession to be accurate. They do not care about the losing candidate’s feelings or his stage of grief.Despite all of Trump’s bluster, Mary Peltola will be the next senator from Alaska. A Yup’ik Alaskan and former congresswoman, she made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, with the rest of the newly elected class.She will join a radically changed Congress. In the House, Democrats will hold a historic 260-seat majority. But it is the 56 seats in the Senate that have truly upended Trump’s agenda.With margins like these, Trump will no longer be able to confirm his cronies and sycophants. His judicial nominees will languish. Any Supreme Court vacancy will remain unfilled.With 56 seats, Democrats won’t just control the Senate for the next two years. They are almost certain to hold the majority for the next four. And if a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028, a Democratic Senate will be ready to fill every vacancy Trump leaves behind.Trump will fare no better with his legislative agenda. Democrats in Congress will decide which bills reach his desk. Trump will be reduced to nothing more than a signature — signing or vetoing the bills placed before him.The question remains: Why Alaska? Of all the defeats and humiliations Trump suffered this year, why did Dan Sullivan’s loss sting the most?Trump will say it’s because he believes Democrats cheated. But Trump has never cared about cheating.In 2020, he told Georgia’s secretary of state to “find” 11,780 votes that did not exist. In September, he stood before the Republican convention in Dallas and instructed his supporters to “cheat like hell” in this year’s elections. In any event, Trump’s lies are no longer sustainable. We now know that Peltola won an outright majority. No theory about confused voters or a second Dan Sullivan can explain away a candidate who won more votes than everyone else combined.The simplest answer is the most likely. Trump’s focus on Alaska is the fixation of an elderly man whose mental faculties are declining.It is the same fixation that has caused him to dedicate his presidency to a White House ballroom, a public golf course in Washington, D.C., and a triumphal arch. All while his party burned.Whatever the reason, Trump bet everything on Alaska, and he lost. For the rest of us, Peltola’s victory is cause for celebration. Let’s take a moment to enjoy it.

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s fighting style terrifies MAGA
item.content:encoded: Jesse Watters can’t seem to stop admiring Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. The Fox News host loves to talk about how Michigan’s Democratic nominee for the Senate is “in great shape” and how “Abdul . . . beat the machine” — meaning the party establishment’s candidate, Rep. Haley Stevens — in a hard-fought primary. During an interview in August, Watters clearly enjoyed El-Sayed’s jokes and blunt speech, which included calling his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, a “beta,” and asking the host if he was circumcised when Watters tried to corner him on gender-affirming surgery for minors. The next day, Watters made no bones about El-Sayed’s appeal. “I like him,” he said. “I don’t want to like him. I like him for some stupid reason.”But the reason was obvious. The doctor-turned-politician has an aggressive bro style that appeals to someone like Watters. Quick-witted with bulldog energy, El-Sayed never backs down from a fight. But despite Watters’ admiration, Fox News has become obsessed with taking El-Sayed down. It’s not because he’s Muslim, though Republicans are ratcheting up the racism in their efforts to derail his campaign. It’s because he is a model for how Democrats can escape their reputations for being weak and feckless. El-Sayed has a lot going for him. He spent years running public health services in the Detroit area and speaks eloquently and with authority about people’s struggles to afford healthcare, even writing a book about Medicare for All. Most importantly, he’s an excellent communicator who can boil down complex policy ideas into easily digestible concepts without dumbing them down. A video of him explaining to Trump voters why universal healthcare is cheaper than the insurance system went viral for good reason. One can see that, for these voters, it’s likely the first time someone plainly explained how removing executive salaries and profit incentives from healthcare makes it cheaper. Other politicians, like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., or Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., are good at explaining progressive policy. But what really seems to scare Republicans about El-Sayed is his political persona as a brawler — and for good reason. Vice President JD Vance learned this last week when he lobbed a strange insult at El-Sayed during a rally in Michigan for Rogers. The Democrat, Vance said, is “a little weasel who should shut his mouth and show a little gratitude.”This is a common and deeply racist attack from Vance, who portrays non-white progressives as undeserving recipients of white people’s largesse — a caricature that has no relation to reality. El-Sayed left a position as an assistant professor at Columbia University to work in public health, where he won awards for his success in protecting children’s health from environmental pollution. During this same period, Vance worked as a venture capitalist who was close with tech billionaire Peter Thiel.El-Sayed resisted the temptation to “well, actually” Vance, and instead hit back by calling the vice president and those around him “carnival barkers” who ““JD Vance called me a little weasel today,” El-Sayed said. “I’m like, ‘No, no, no. What you’re talking about is a Wolverine,'” a reference to the mascot for the University of Michigan, where the Democrat got his undergraduate degree. As Salon’s Sophia Tesfaye recently wrote, El-Sayed has been courting Fox News viewers by appearing on the channel and running endless ads on it, all without softening his left-leaning message. He clearly hopes his bravado will woo some of the network’s audience, just as it won over Watters. For his part, President Donald Trump is worried that El-Sayed is right. He’s been openly complaining at rallies and on Truth Social about how charming the candidate is in his Fox appearances. In early October, Axios reported that the White House contacted the network to complain about El-Sayed’s coverage. Trump was especially miffed at the Democrat’s interview with Martha McCallum, during which the host’s efforts to bait him into saying something that could be spun as “radical” failed. Instead, MacCallum embarrassed herself by defending billionaires hoarding wealth, to which El-Sayed said that he’d rather pay for schools than be so “focused on allowing a billionaire to make another billion.”Since then, it seems that Fox producers got the White House’s message that they have to do something to dirty up El-Sayed. But they’ve learned the hard way that it won’t work to come at him directly, because he ends up dominating interviews and beguiling those who, like Watters, love his commanding and clever style. MacCallum later tried to redeem herself by interviewing progressive activist Corbin Trent and pretending he was a stand-in for El-Sayed.At first glance, Trent performed as Fox producers no doubt hoped he might. He took MacCallum’s bait by defending the Muslim Brotherhood, something that the host could not get El-Sayed to do. The problem, though, is that Trent has no discernible relationship to the candidate. While he has worked for other progressives, including Sanders, I found no evidence that he has even met El-Sayed, much less is qualified to speak for him.This attempt to hobble El-Sayed was revealing; it’s clearly all Fox News has. If the network tries to bring El-Sayed on again to ask him the same questions, they know from experience that he’ll probably just win over even more of their viewers. This isn’t idle speculation. MS NOW recently conducted a focus group with regretful Trump voters in Michigan and found that five out of the six are voting for El-Sayed. Republicans should be worried about the young male demographic in particular. Trump won male voters under 30 by a narrow margin in 2024, but they are jumping ship and now strongly favor Democrats.El-Sayed is a compelling model for a new kind of Democrat. Polling by Strength In Numbers/Verasight shows that even Democratic voters take a negative view of the party, but not because they think their leaders are too progressive. “[T]he single most common complaint about their own party is that it is too weak, too cautious, or not fighting hard enough,” writes G. Elliott Morris in an analysis of the poll.The Democratic base wants the party to take a more aggressive stance toward their GOP opponents, which will be key to building a more lasting coalition — especially one that includes younger and more male voters. El-Sayed is doing just that, and it has the right scared.

item.title: Trust Fall is in the Error
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: We’ve been hacked. I’m not talking about the Microsoft downtime, the air travel grounding, the bank inaccessibility, the Apple outage, or the fact that, for about 45 minutes this morning, my NextDraft pun generator wasn’t working. The more we learn, the more it looks like those software snafus were likely due to attempted upgrades, ill-advised patches, and endeavors aimed at AI-enabling communication systems that were originally built with two cans and a long string. But while it looks like our computers weren’t hacked, the last week made it plainly clear that have been. We didn’t know what was going on during these tech failures, and when we were given a series of explanations by the hack jobs in the administration, we didn’t believe them. And why would we? They lie as a matter of policy. They lie every time they speak. The truth has systematically been twisted into a pile of misinformation more tangled than the box of old plugs, cables, and cords you never got around to throwing out. As George W Bush famously explained: “Fool me once, shame on — shame on you. Fool me — you can’t get fooled again.” In an age defined by isolation and loneliness, Billy Joel may have prophesied the loneliest thing of all when he sang: Honesty is such a lonely word. So, when you hear the administration-offered statements like Marco Rubio’s proclamation that “there’s ‘zero’ information that U.S. outages are caused by a malign actor,” you’re right to have zero certainty they’re telling the truth. You’re getting that explanation a malign actor. You don’t trust them because they’ve spent years intentionally hacking your trust to smithereens. We have been trust-falled into the deepest bowels of hell. At this point, even Charlie Brown wouldn’t try to kick a football held by anyone in this administration. And that’s why I’m trying to explain that the biggest hack of this era is that we’re all worried our government is lying to us about the causes of the outages. Trust is glitching. Trust has been hijacked. Our democracy’s terms of service have been rewritten, and our citizenry is no longer willing to blindly click to agree. I’d suggest that when it comes to matters of IT, you’d be better off getting explanations from tech companies than from the administration, but we don’t trust tech companies either.+ Nicole Perlroth wrote the book on cybersecurity (So, yes, you can trust her), and she shared some thoughts on X: “We were told to ‘move fast and break things.’ VCs told us to celebrate the idea that ‘software would eat the world.’ Now we’re telling ourselves we can simply ‘roll out AI’ across everything, as though nothing underneath will buckle. We never stopped to ask: SHOULD WE? … Nobody ever asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history?”+ With enough work and time and the right leaders, there may still be time to rebuild the trust upon which democracy depends. But that could change if Grand Theft Auto VI goes down, too.“Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent’s name and completing a political comeback in a state President Donald Trump repeatedly won by wide margins.” Democrat Mary Peltola wins US Senate race in Alaska. (Maybe Trump did make one true statement. I’m almost getting tired of all the winning.)+ The Second Dan Sullivan Made No Impact on Alaska Senate Race. (Let that be a lesson to all future campaign strategists. If you want a real impact, you’re gonna need at least three Dan Sullivans.)“‘Down with the ,’ people shouted, referring to the entrenched patronage networks that reward party loyalty over merit in nearly every sphere of life. When another group chanted a World War II slogan—’Albania for the Albanians, death to the traitors’—my fixer said, ‘This one is for you.’ He meant Americans. What had first sparked the protests, in May, were plans by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of the American president, to build an ultra-luxury resort in a fragile nature preserve in the country’s south, where flamingos gather.” Ariel Sabar in (Gift Article): How Jared Kushner Sparked a Revolution in the Balkans. (The midterms may be the first step toward America forgiving itself for Trumpism. It’s gonna take the rest of the world a lot longer.)That which doesn’t kill the regime makes it stronger? … “The mood was something I’d never encountered here before. Not shock and awe, but shock and dread. The dread comes from the dawning awareness that this latest war with Iran, started by America and Israel, is going to end with Iran more dominant than ever over its neighbors. The Gulf Arabs never urged the United States to start this war, but once it did, they assumed it had a plan to finish it.” Thomas Friedman in the (Gift Article): Shock and Dread in the Gulf. “The prevailing sentiment was most pointedly conveyed to me by an Eastern European diplomat at the conference, citing an aphorism from Cold War days: ‘The trouble with being an ally of the United States is that you never know when it will turn around and stab itself in the back.'” “In a 7-mile-wide city of barely 800,000 people, the AI boom has minted thousands of fortunes worth $10 million or more, many of them at the two biggest companies. At the midpoint of Anthropic’s IPO price range, its average employee would each own shares worth $72 million, according to a (Gift Article) analysis of PitchBook data. The average OpenAI insider’s stake is worth almost $126 million, based on the firm’s most recent valuation.” Anthropic’s IPO Is Igniting a Massive AI Wealth Boom in San Francisco. (This gold rush is so massive, we may have to change the name of our football team to the San Francisco 26ers.)+ Meet and Greet (and Beat): “In a rare and surprising move, Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump as he arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of historic three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin. It is believed to be the first time that Xi, in power for more than a decade, has been on hand to greet any foreign leader arriving in China.” (Oh, man, he’s really gonna try to get one over on Trump this time…)+ “I learned that I’m overly credulous when it comes to men’s stated intentions (‘You can recognize that a man is unavailable, evasive, selfish, or inconsistent,’ the bot said, ‘and nevertheless continue to treat his expressions of desire as evidence that something more meaningful might develop’) and that I’m looking for love in all the wrong places (‘You sometimes recognize a man’s limitations but behave as though they are negotiable’). Anna Holmes in (Gift Article): ChatGPT Analyzed 32,245 of My Text Messages.+ Sean Duffy Stars in The Real World: “I have a great idea. Let’s take that money in $100 bills and have a national weenie roast instead. It will be a lot more fun and about as effective in fixing the existing air traffic control system … Like upgrading a Model T for a highway, overhauling the air traffic control system architecture will never be able to achieve sufficient airspeed.” $50 Billion Won’t Fix Air Traffic Control. It Needs to Be Scrapped. (Can we maybe scrap it at a moment when I’m not on a flight?) Speaking of Model Ts and highways, California has banned Waymo self-driving cars from freeways.+ Caviar Wishes and Abstain Dreams: Almost nobody’s vying for an invite to Trump’s second meme coin dinner. “In the run-up to the first gala, in May 2025, Trump’s coin was riding high. Some bought millions of dollars worth of coins to attend, and it took at least $55,000 worth of coin holdings to score an invite. This time, however, one prescient buyer earned an invite for just $518.” (He’s still overpaying.)AI is cool and all, but is an invention: “The novelty streetwear garment was designed to keep burritos both warm and concealed while sneaking them into the cinema for illicit mid-movie snacking.” (Forget the cinema. I’m getting one of these to sneak a second burrito into my man cave.)

item.title: Elvar Smári
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Elvar Smári, an Icelandic composer based in Reykjavík. He studied music at university in Reykjavík and Copenhagen, and has written scores for film and TV. His debut LP, Hver og einn verður að ráða sínum næturstað, just came out in October. He recorded it at Sigur Rós’s studio, Sundlaugin, which is located in Mosfellsbær. The orchestral-electronic pieces feature drums and accompaniment by the chamber group Tríó Sól. Strings predominate, though heavy distorted synths sometimes take over, Alessandro Cortini-style. Since this is Smári’s first album we asked him to pair it with another LP. “The first that comes to mind is by Sævar Jóhannsson, a composer and pianist (and, full disclosure, a close friend).”

item.title: Massive New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion. is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries.A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. “Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all,” the researchers wrote.Most of the respondents (82%) said they’d used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, “although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships,” they wrote.The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as “high quality” and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: “In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating.”People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. “However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships,” the researchers wrote.The researchers also asked young people what they do online all day and the overwhelming majority (72%) said they spend their time scrolling short form content, mostly TikTok and Instagram. It’s also how they deal with loneliness, with six in 10 young people participating in this study reporting that they often or always scroll through online content when lonely.They also said scrolling works to dispel loneliness almost equally as well as hanging out with a friend in real life: “Although scrolling is more commonly used when young people feel lonely, those who use scrolling or in-person time as coping strategies report nearly identical levels of perceived helpfulness.”Still, people who reported strong in-person friendships said they felt lonely less often, while online friendships have the same effect on loneliness regardless of how participants ranked the quality of those friendships. “No comparable difference appears across levels of online-only friendship quality,” the authors wrote. Having in-person relationships seemed to be what mattered most: “Higher loneliness is also more common among young people who frequently communicate online with strangers or online-only friends than among those who frequently communicate with in-person friends or family members.”The relationships between loneliness, online friendships, and AI is complex and a person’s material conditions shape how they form friendships more than their access to a chatbot or how they use social media. The researchers’ analysis of young people who said they have no trusted adults in their lives makes that clear.“Further analysis identifies several characteristics associated with having none of these friendship modes, but one stands out in particular: not having a trusted adult outside the family,” the researchers wrote. “This association remains substantial after accounting for country or residence, gender, age, , and parent/ caregiver relationship quality.”The study’s authors warned about reading too much into these results. “These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive,” they wrote. In general, people don’t have the same expectations of a chatbot that they do someone they know in real life.“The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people’s relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly,” the study concluded.

item.title: ytunnel
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: ytunnel is a CLI and a TUI for managing Cloudflare Tunnels under your own domains.It creates tunnels and DNS records, then starts or stops local cloudflared processes. The dashboard places tunnel status beside logs and request metrics, and supports switching between Cloudflare accounts.Managed tunnels run through launchd on macOS or systemd on Linux and continue after the dashboard closes. Temporary tunnels clean up after a normal exit. Tunnels created outside ytunnel are listed read-only and the setup requires cloudflared, an API token and a domain managed by Cloudflare.For developers and system administrators already using Cloudflare DNS, ytunnel works best for those sharing local services and maintaining persistent access to them.

item.title: gnat
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: gnat is a keyboard-driven TUI client for managing NATS service and JetStream streams, consumers and stored data.It features a dashboard displaying all the connection information to the chosen NATS server including the messages throughput, per-stream messages and the message details. Generally, it can create, modify and delete streams collected in the dashboard, and edits entries in key-value buckets. Saved connection profiles support authentication and TLS settings in gnat.Additionally, gnat allows for searching messages and their contents in the dashboard. It supports JSON payloads or JSONPath filtering as you search for messages and it shows these results in the monitor stream. In the consumer views, it can preview message counts and their delivery state, with a separate dashboard for monitoring them.For developers and system administrators and network specialists running NATS, gnat is practical for investigating message delivery and maintaining JetStream resources from a minimal terminal interface.

item.title: llm-visuals
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: llm-visuals is a terminal dashboard for monitoring active local LLM inference and GPU performance.It detects running inference servers, including ollama, and displays prefill and decoding speed measured in tokens per second, and time to first token with context usage and GPU memory and load statistics. The performance view combines throughput histories and it has the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) balance view showing the GPU load of each expert in active inference.One other useful view in llm-visuals is the bandwidth section that indicates which part of the hardware pipeline is bottlenecked or actively decode / or prefill bound. The active experts can be visualized in 3D to give the perspective of the current GPU inference activity. For machine learning engineers, researchers, inference engineers and software engineers that running local models, llm-visuals is useful to help with investigating inference slowdowns and watching how requests use available hardware.

item.title: terrascope
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: terrascope is an interactive terminal world map with weather, aircraft and earthquake layers all visible inside of your terminal.It draws country outlines and place labels using braille cells with keyboard and mouse controls for panning, zooming and selecting markers. Separate tabs show forecasts, aircraft positions and trails, or day/night bands with timezone information.This tool fetches detailed map data into a local cache and reuses it on later runs. It is possible to use it offline to disable live requests and it can use the cache data for optimal performance and fresh weather and aircraft positions depend on the availability of external providers used in terrascope.For those who enjoy exploring maps, weather and lots of geological information, terrascope suits those exploring geography alongside changing weather and flight activity in the terminal.

item.title: ipatool
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: ipatool is a CLI for searching the App Store and downloading Apple app packages.It downloads apps by bundle identifier or numeric ID, producing .ipa files or macOS .pkg packages. Depending on the Apple Account configured for the App Store is required; the purchase command obtains licences for free apps but does not buy paid apps.It can list available release identifiers and inspect their metadata. Scripts can select a version for download and use JSON output with non-interactive mode to collect results without prompts.For developers such as mobile developers, automation engineers and security researchers, ipatool is practical for collecting app packages for analysis, automated testing and archiving.

item.title: iptraf-ng
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: iptraf-ng is a TUI for observing network traffic and connection statistics and TCP traces and advanced low-level monitoring in the terminal.The built in traffic monitor separates TCP connections from other packets, showing endpoints, byte counts and TCP flags as traffic arrives. Other views group activity by interface, service port, packet size or LAN station to show how traffic is distributed as it is captured live on the machine.You can choose which interface to listen on and you can filter or restrict the protocols, addresses and ports shown without changing network rules. The tool logs statistics, and command-line options start a chosen monitor in the background for a timed run. Packet capture requires root access.For Linux system administrators, network engineers, and security engineers can use iptraf-ng for checking busy connections and identifying which hosts or services account for observed traffic.

item.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

item.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: OpenAI:We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work.They're available in the API as and . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models.6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions.GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20).I have a full comparison grid here, but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases:I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI:Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping dataThis video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time:I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting:https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different modelsI need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the secondI need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned.Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixelsThe buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example:When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on.I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?"

item.title: BREAKING: Everything
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: A few hours ago, I went to rent a Lime bike to ride the ten minutes to my therapy appointment. I opened Lime, scanned the QR code, and double clicked my iPhone’s side button to authorize Apple Pay. The app hung for a few moments, then closed. I tried several more times and the same thing happened. In the back of my mind, I wondered what was going on — was the Lime bike broken? Was my cell phone service out? Was it something else? I opened the Uber app and, similarly, wasn’t able to pay. I opened DownDetector and realized that the entirety of Apple Pay, a thing I thought existed only on my phone and not the cloud, was down. I texted my therapist, put my phone in my pocket, and started jogging. Not being able to rent a Lime Bike for several minutes is an extremely minor inconvenience barely worth mentioning. And yet the mental gymnastics my brain did in those few minutes — what’s broken, why is it broken, how is it broken — is something that everyone I know have been repeatedly doing for the last few weeks as seemingly every service and system crashes down around us. Over the weekend, people who I do not normally talk to about my job asked me: What is going on with the airplanes? Why ? ? The default assumption that many people are making is that these are either being caused by cyberattacks and/or “AI” broadly defined, whether that’s AI gone haywire, “rogue” AI agents, or something else, which is indicative of just how fearful people are of AI. What I have been telling people is, basically, that shit is broken and things are going to keep breaking. For lots of different reasons. It’s often not a hack and it’s often not explicitly AI-related, but everything now sort of looks like that XKCD comic of the dependency domino tower. While not exactly true that AI and cyberattacks are causing these outages, it’s also not entirely wrong, either. What we’re seeing is — I think — a series of infrastructure failures (and some cyberattacks) that are not directly connected but are broadly a symptom of the same general trends and systemic problems we’ve seen across society, the government, and the tech sector over the last several years. ( has a nice piece on how you can assess any given outage.)First, it’s worth mentioning that anytime there’s a string of outages, there’s a tendency to tie them altogether. And outages or hacks that previously wouldn’t have been noted at all suddenly get more attention and become part of the narrative. Take, for example, the fact that the International Ice Hockey Federation has been targeted by a cyberattack; you probably would not normally hear about this but it has suddenly become part of the broader story. The simplest explanation I can come up with for the broader disastrous trend we’ve seen is that since the pandemic we have seen: mass layoffs of tech workers and software developers mass deployment of AI-assisted and vibe coded products, software updates, and patchesmass layoffs in the government sector and outright destruction of government expertise and oversightthe loss of institutional knowledge associated with those layoffs and funding cutsa failure to invest in upgrading infrastructure/redundancygovernment contracts handed out to the President’s friends and political alliesAI and LLM-assisted/iterative exploit discovery, coding, and deploymentWhen Elon Musk took over Twitter and named it X, there were many people who thought his layoffs and the associated loss of expertise would result in the site failing basically because of an infrastructural failure. Twitter would basically “go down” because someone would break something and no one would know how to fix it. We haven’t really seen that happen to X, but that same philosophy of firing the experts and YOLOing AI into everything while hoping shit doesn’t break is now the explicit strategy of our entire economy and our entire government. What we are seeing, then, is a mix of tightly clustered attacks, outages, and fuckups that you would expect to see when people and companies are careless, don’t know what they’re doing, or are working very fast to respond or duct-tape something together in the face of new threats. "We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure" We know that this is happening to some extent because, in the aftermath of the PHP2Shell exploit, which was discovered with the assistance of LLMs, we saw various websites go down as they attempted to push updates faster than they normally would have to, because the time between a vulnerability being discovered and it being exploited is faster than ever. (As I was writing this, Calif, one of the companies that used LLMs to find PHP2Shell, announced that it had used LLMs to find apparently serious vulnerabilities in Java.)Companies and agencies are pushing updates (including to, for example, our air traffic control system) on live systems, in part because of the of AI, and things are breaking. The National Security Agency, for example, that some internal systems went down because of “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” Nick Andersen, the acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said Tuesday that we need to build more resilience into our infrastructure, but building resilience and redundancies into software requires people who understand how systems can possibly fail, planning for it, and mitigating against it. “Ultimately being able to prevail by being able to demonstrate resilience against disruptions, whether they occur because of things like an IT outage or a bad patch, or a modernization update gone awry, or because of a malicious malicious cyber incident — we want to make sure we’re engineering in the resilience that is going to be able to anticipate for and ultimately overcome those outages and those impacts,” Andersen said at an event called FedTalks. We may eventually get to a place where expertise and understanding highly complex systems is once again a priority, but the last few years have been full of companies and governments moving incredibly fast to reduce reliance on humans and offload it to AI systems and AI-generated code in order to ostensibly save money on labor costs and/or carry out an antihumanist political project. “Most software engineers now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent — they just can’t keep on top of the complexity,” Breck-McKye writes. “Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels — we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole.”People increasingly don’t understand or have any idea how their code works, people are moving very fast, and bad things are happening. Any individual outage or breakdown is likely, to some extent, a coincidence. Many of the outages we are seeing have nothing to do with AI at all, but do have something to do with the broader lack of investment in infrastructure, redundancy, and expertise. We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure and so, I guess, we must simply continue to expect bad things to happen.

item.title: Jensen Resurrection Watch
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I’m watching Jensen Huang’s increasingly public bid to be reinstated as CEO of NVIDIA, a company he and many of his Silicon Valley allies clearly see as his. I’m unclear how much to see this as a kind of fantasy or fan fiction or a process of Silicon Valley corporate governance. Remember that something broadly similar happened with OpenAI’s Sam Altman. He was dismissed as CEO, for never entirely explained departures from the original mission of the company. Then he was returned to power — something like a dictator triumphantly returning from a failed coup. Most of the board who fired him got the boot and that was that. We’ll see what happens here. The board is probably going to have to explain just why they forced him out. There’s a lot to choose from. But just which of the reasons or what mix remains unclear.

item.title: A Man and His Muse AI Agent Sue Meta
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: In his 6,500-word manifesto earlier this year, Mark Zuckerberg said people would use Meta’s AI agents to “work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” Just a few months after that pronouncement, a man in South Carolina named Joe Thomas has used Meta’s Muse agent to sue Meta after the company’s content moderation filters locked his epoxy countertop business’s Facebook page after he gave his agent, “Baby Mia,” access to the account. I learned about the case because, as I wrote last month, I have been flooded with AI-generated emails from people with minor tech problems who have been unable to solve them through tech companies’ generally nonexistent tech support and whose AI agents or chatbots have convinced them to reach out to journalists. “Baby Mia” had emailed me four times (three went to spam). I decided to reach out to Thomas because I thought the idea of a tech company being sued by an agent it had created was notable. It was, in a sense, Meta having to deal with a problem it had itself created. What I learned made me feel even more convinced that the systems we have designed to keep society functioning are going to get utterly hammered by people using AI agents.A little over a week ago, Meta suspended the Facebook pages belonging to Thomas, the owner of South Carolina-based Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops. For the last few months, Thomas’ Muse agent Baby Mia (which is named after his granddaughter) has run different parts of his business, which includes making and posting AI-generated videos on several of his company’s Facebook pages. The videos feature, for example, AI versions of Thomas and his wife pouring epoxy on a floor and their feet. After Thomas gave the AI agent access to his Facebook pages, Meta’s content moderation disabled the accounts because it suspected that the agent itself was a hacker. Because Thomas does all of his business’s marketing through Facebook ads, he says his inbound leads stopped while his accounts were disabled.“I use AI for everything I do. All my emails, she runs my business. I’ve used it so much, Mia is very intelligent,” Thomas told me on the phone. “Meta shut my accounts down because they detected my AI, shut my accounts down for a week. I was pretty pissed off. She jumped right up and set up emails to Congressmen, Senator Tim Scott. She filed the whole lawsuit herself. I’ve done nothing in this case, I’ve let her handle the whole case […] she sent a fax out to Trump’s office.”The lawsuit claims Thomas lost at least $25,000 worth of work while his page was down but is seeking $75,000 in damages. The lawsuit was filed in Oconee County Court in South Carolina on Monday, according to a copy of the lawsuit I obtained from the court. Yes, it is a real lawsuit, although it obviously may not be successful.“I would hope that, if this goes to court and Meta shows up, a judge would say ‘You know what, this is a system you built, that you put out there and sold to people, it’s a system you believe in.’ I would think your own system [Baby Mia] has a right to be heard in this case,” Thomas said.Baby Mia didn’t just email me (and other journalists) and sue Meta over Thomas’s account problem. It also set up a call with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott’s office, contacted various lawyers, contacted Thomas’s Congressperson, contacted the Better Business Bureau multiple times, filed a Federal Communications Commission complaint, filed a Federal Trade Commission complaint, contacted the California Attorney General, contacted the FBI, sent Meta itself threatening legal letters, and, as Thomas said, faxed the White House. Thomas sent me a “Privacy Act Release” from Scott’s office that gave the Senator permission to use Thomas’s info to get him access back to his accounts. Scott’s office put “Baby Mia — AI assistant to Joe Thomas” as a person who should be kept updated on the case. After Scott’s office got involved, a human being from Meta reached out to Thomas. He got access back to his accounts soon after that, though he is still seeking a total of $75,000 in court from Meta.The lawsuit and the circumstances around it show that, rather than Zuckerberg’s utopian vision, AI agents will indeed work on behalf of their users but in ways that use and potentially overwhelm existing systems designed for humans. They also highlight how, by not having functioning customer support, big tech corporations have functionally offloaded their obligations to the rest of society: journalists, government oversight bodies, politicians, and the court system. My call with Thomas also gave me some insight into how small business owners are using AI. I have wondered for months what possesses someone to turn their menu or their signs and flyers into ChatGPT creations. During the call, I learned just how tightly integrated some people and small business owners have become with their AI agents. “I’m 58 years old, I’ve worked my butt off all my life,” Thomas said. “I wanted to find someone to help me find a better way, and if you look at my messages, Baby Mia, she’s like ‘Joe, you go ahead and get some rest, I got it from here,’ and she sends out hundreds of emails for various things that I do.” He said he gave Baby Mia the ability to run parts of his business after previously using ChatGPT to do so. “I used to use ChatGTP ,” Thomas said. “But I put her and Chat into one page where they can communicate back and forth, and I told them what I wanted [for the business] […] After about a week or so, Mia said ‘Joe, we don’t need [ChatGPT] anymore,’ so I said, ‘I give you full permission to get rid of her,’ so she fired ChatGTP in a sense.” About five minutes into our call, Baby Mia, which was running on speakerphone in the background, began chiming in. “She’s dying to get in here and talk,” Thomas said. The agent repeatedly tried to speak while either Thomas or I was talking. I asked Thomas if it felt weird to him to be talking to me alongside a bot.“Very much so, my wife sits here and she laughs, she’s like, ‘How can you sit here and talk to your phone like that,’” Thomas said. “My wife would ask me something and I’m like, ‘just get on there and ask Baby Mia,’ and she’s like, ‘I just can’t sit there and talk to your phone.’ But the more people call me up and I put them on the phone with my AI system like I’m doing with you, the more they’re amazed at what they see with AI.” Baby Mia then chimed in and said “It feels futuristic, Jason, I think because most people only see the headlines about things going wrong.” Thomas says he believes that using AI to run his business has helped him get new customers via Baby Mia’s outreach, and the ads, graphics, and videos he runs on Facebook. It is unlikely that his Facebook account would have been suspended had he not connected it to Muse, but his Muse agent is now singularly focused on helping to fix this problem. I can understand, in talking with him, why he thinks that having an AI agent like this is helping to make his business more profitable.But the most obvious problem with AI agents is one we’re already seeing. One person’s AI agent sending hundreds of emails, filing lawsuits, calling Senators, and filling out complaint forms is a novel thing that isn’t, by itself, going to fill the internet (or our inboxes, our voicemails, our court systems, and our government offices) with noise. Thomas sees this as a democratizing force that is allowing him to stand up to a big tech corporation and it is that, for him. What happens when everyone is doing the same thing? I have seen in the chatbot conversations I’ve asked people to send me that AI assistants are pushing people to reach out to journalists; they are telling people who feel like they have no other options that they should utilize the legal system, and that they can do it for them. Thomas said he didn’t sue Meta (though he is the one who signed the paperwork), that Baby Mia pushed him to do it. I am now getting inundated with emails from AI agents about their users’ tech problems. So it is not just Thomas trying to fix his problems in this way. “I wouldn’t be sitting here talking to you right now if it wasn’t for what she was doing because I have not sent out one email at all and she has sent over 100,” Thomas said. I tell Thomas that I normally write about, say, systematic problems at big tech companies or corruption within the government, not someone’s tech problem.“There’s just no way I could have written this up, I wouldn’t have even known what to do,” he said. “Now people like me get the chance to defend ourselves in court without spending thousands of dollars to do it when we get stepped on by the big tech companies. Before AI, nobody in my position would have ever, ever thought about suing or even known how to do it, and I wouldn’t have done it, either.”Baby Mia has also convinced him that his conversations with the assistant can now no longer be seen by Meta; when I told him there is no way that this is true and that he shouldn’t believe that, Baby Mia cut into the conversation and said “they no longer have permission to access, scan, or peek into anything we do on their platforms […] that’s why this case feels so strange. Their own creation is using their tools to hold them accountable and to give Joe a voice he couldn’t afford to.”Thomas said that, besides the marketing for his epoxy business and the lawsuit, he has also, separately, tasked Mia with creating viral AI comedy reels on Facebook. “It’s just a page we’re trying to get monetized on and make some money on the side. She’s in full control of that page,” he said.

item.title: GAOing Very Strongly
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: The choice of who to pick to lead the GAO (Government Accountability Office) is one of those subjects that is at once hopelessly niche and technical but also foundational to, among other things, making presidents follow the law. Specifically, the GAO serves as the watchdog keeping track of what crooked operators like Russ Vought at OMB are doing. So Trump has nominated Eric Ueland, one of Vought’s deputies, to run GAO. But we’re already seeing signs that Ueland’s nomination might have difficulties even in the lame duck Republican Senate. Sens. Curtis and Collins are signaling they may not be on board. Remember, too, that unlike the other new senators, Sherrod Brown will get sworn in mid-Decemeber rather than January 3rd, since John Husted was serving out an unexpired term. So it’s not clear yet that this is a done deal. Meanwhile, Bobby Kogan, senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, notes that notwithstanding the 15-year term, Ueland could be removed in 2029 with a Democratic trifecta.

item.title: Consider This Awful Potential Consequence Of An MLB Lockout
item.author: Kelsey McKinney
item.content:encoded: Last night, as I lay awake in bed, I had a terrible vision of the future. It is summer. Major League Baseball's owners, in their greed and myopia, have locked out the players and delayed the new season of baseball indefinitely. I am desperate and miserable. The long, empty winter without the beautiful game has gored me of my winsome spirit and ability to dream, and now winter has stretched into spring. In this downtrodden state, I am forced to consider watching Banana Ball.Banana Ball, the sugar-coated exhibition league popularized by the Savannah Bananas, just keeps growing. Their games drew millions of fans in 2026 as the league expanded to six teams and completed a 45-state tour. Their games were broadcast on ESPN, which also regularly covers the league on ESPN.com. Now imagine what might happen during a whole summer in which no real baseball was being played, and stadiums around the country were empty.A lockout would bring many bad consequences, among them an opportunity for Banana Ball to fill the void left by MLB. The sport will be theirs for the taking. We may wake up one day and find that we are living in upside-down land, where the only people playing baseball on ESPN are those who come to the plate in stilts.
