item.title: Chargers Achieve Bare Minimum Of Dignity
item.author: Samer Kalaf
item.content:encoded: You can call the Los Angeles Chargers many things: hopeless, depressing to think about, an ideal candidate for contraction. This blog could end right here and no one would think it was strange. But after Monday night's 23-20 victory over the Baltimore Ravens, you cannot call the Chargers winless.Before the season began, Chargers-Ravens seemed decent on paper as a national broadcast: two mid-tier AFC teams that should have been in playoff contention in Week 10. Alas, there was a lot of football to be played between then and now. Significant injuries to quarterbacks Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley effectively wrapped up Baltimore's season a couple of weeks ago. Apparently, Joe Fagnano was not the answer. The promise of the Ravens' 4-1 start has fully evaporated, and the rest of the AFC North simply looks better than them. Their best hope is somehow being reassigned to the NFC South within the next month.As for the Chargers ... woof. They lost eight straight games and grew increasingly appalling each week. QB Justin Herbert regressed so hard that it left a crater. Head coach Jim Harbaugh began to spend a significant amount of his time either issuing votes of confidence to various parties, or lobbying for his continued employment, as well as that of his new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, who has firmly established that he's only a few letters away from Mike McCoy. Earlier this month, Chargers tight end Charlie Kolar was informed that the team's offense had gone 37 straight drives without scoring a touchdown, and he was visibly distraught. When I wrote their Why Your Team Sucks entry this summer, I felt a little hesitation in dumping so much on what was an 11-win team last season, but it turns out I didn't dump nearly enough.

item.title: Buster Posey Is Our New Hall Of Fame Debate Topic
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: As an objective standard, baseball's Hall of Fame season provides a better list of managers and executives than players this year, which surely provides some wintry comfort for people who favor polo shirts, sunglasses, and a phone pressed against an ear while making frowny faces.But "objective standard" and the Hall of Fame have always been estranged, as should probably be the case. The only actually indisputable term here is "hall," because the physical plant is indeed that. Everything else is based on personal taste, and you can't have personal taste without persons, and you can't have persons without accepting that their version of objectivity typically begins with them objecting to someone else's version of same. It's how family fights over the holidays were invented.But your issues with your dimwitted cousin grabbing the last anything on the table are not why we're here. Buster Posey is, and oddly enough, so are Brian Sabean and Bruce Bochy. This is a circumstantially skewed San Francisco Bay Area-centered Hall of Fame season, especially when you add Dusty Baker and Sandy Alderson, but it's far less of a stretch to imagine Sabean and Bochy in particular being voted in by the Contemporary Baseball Committee than any of the players by the general electorate—despite the fact that Sabean and Bochy may not get into the Hall without Posey.

item.title: Oh No, The Phones
item.author: Sebastian Stockman
item.content:encoded: Mom’s phone number was 620. If a friend wanted to reach her on her family’s farm just outside the rural Missouri town of Alma (pop. 400, more or less), they had to buzz the operator at the Alma Telephone Company and ask for the Corders or say, “Give me 620, please.” The operator, who probably knew by heart which circuit the Corders were on, would ring line No. 6 with the prescribed sequence: two long rings, zero short rings. The phones in 10 or so households all along the party line would let loose, with the ring pattern signaling to the other farmsteads that the call was for the Corder household. But anyone who wanted to pick it up could—and sometimes did.“You could usually tell when somebody else was on the line,” Mom said. Most often that somebody was Grandma Dieckhoff, who lived one house down the line with her son’s family. The ever-present possibility of eavesdroppers disciplined Mom’s high school chatter—except when it supercharged it: “We sometimes exaggerated a little to give her something to talk about.”Mom remembers precisely when her parents finally got off the party line, much later than most of the U.S.: December 1972, her freshman year at the University of Missouri. Late-adopting Alma Telephone skipped over rotary phones altogether, heading straight to direct dial. Grandma and Grandpa called her up, marveling at the ability simply to punch in 10 numbers to reach her, and only her.

item.title: Why Rich People Used To Collect Unicorn Horns
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: During the Renaissance, spurred by the accelerating arrival of items from all over the world, wealthy Europeans began assembling handcrafted curios and unusual artifacts from the natural world in wonder cabinets, or wunderkammers. In this video, Evan Puschak takes a look at how this practice evolved and what it says about that period in history.This was the period of the scientific revolution when thinkers were re-evaluating their reliance on ancient wisdom in the light of all the novel things arriving daily from around the world. “What grounds were there,” Steven Chapen writes, “for crediting ancient limits on the stock of factual knowledge? Every day, new phenomena presented themselves about which the ancient texts were silent.”What was needed for the growth of real knowledge, according to philosophers like Francis Bacon, was not an interpretation of old texts, but an inventory of new facts.A Web log really, then, is a Wunderkammer. That is to say, the genealogy of Web logs points not to the world of letters but to the early history of museums — to the “cabinet of wonders,” or Wunderkammer, that marked the scientific landscape of Renaissance modernity: a random collection of strange, compelling objects, typically compiled and owned by a learned, well-off gentleman. A set of ostrich feathers, a few rare shells, a South Pacific coral carving, a mummified mermaid — the Wunderkammer mingled fact and legend promiscuously, reflecting European civilization’s dazed and wondering attempts to assimilate the glut of physical data that science and exploration were then unleashing.Just so, the Web log reflects our own attempts to assimilate the glut of immaterial data loosed upon us by the “discovery” of the networked world.Some 26 years later, I still think about kottke.org that way. I mean, what is the Video Closet if not a cabinet of wonders?

item.title: The Trump White House Can Run from Real Congressional Oversight But It Can’t Hide
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: As usual, there’s no one prism through which to see the upcoming fight over Democrats daring to conduct congressional oversight — but the best prism is that the Trump White House just wants to run out the clock until the end of his term.Yes, it’s also fundamentally a continuation of the administration’s subordination of Congress in contravention of the constitutional order (except that it no longer has a supine GOP Congress to run over). It’s also an effort to save the administration’s political neck by blocking further revelations of corruption and wrongdoing. It’s also an attempt to project dominance and assert control at a time of acute political weakness.But most of all, it’s an attempt to buy time.The Trump administration is going to throw up an incredible amount of chaff to delay, obscure, and knock Democrats — but especially the political press — off track. It started with the absurd campaign to frame winning Democrats’ promises of congressional oversight as criminal threat. It continues with new Trump Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requiring that every government official and agency obtain White House approval before testifying before Congress. It will soon devolve into refusing to comply with congressional subpoenas, raising preposterous objections, and asserting flimsy claims of privilege, especially executive privilege.We know what’s coming on that front. It’s clear as can be. And it will be an easy pissing match for the press to cover. But it’s not a winnable fight for congressional Democrats: They can’t prevail in court in the 18 months they have to engage in the fight. Plus, the fight itself doesn’t really tell an especially compelling political story that serves the public interest or their own political interest.When viewed in that light, the initial inclination is to figure out how congressional Dems can speed things up and prevent the administration from simply stonewalling until its time in office is up. But at a practical level there are probably only marginal gains to be had on speed, mainly in not dilly dallying before launching the first waves of oversight. Pursuing unwinnable fights would be frustrating and demoralizing.So if you can’t speed it up, then what to do?The more practical approach for the Democratic Congress is to be very clear about what it aims to achieve with oversight, realistic about what is possible, and relentless in pursuing those aims in every available way. (They should still push for maximum speed and take the administration to court to keep the pressure on and eventually, maybe with a different Supreme Court, reassert its authority within the constitutional order. But that should be seen as a necessary line of attack — but not centered as the primary one.)The primary lines of attack should be the ones that best tell a story of the retribution, corruption, and destruction of the Trump II presidency — and which can be told without overly relying on the tools of congressional oversight that are going to be the least useful to the purpose: subpoenas of the Trump administration and hauling in Trump officials for public hearings.The Trump White House is eager for opportunities to confront Congress over process and procedure, like resisting subpoenas. It will savor chances like public hearings to confront elected Democrats directly and defy them in public with absurd behavior that rejects the very premise of congressional oversight. It’s all drearily predictable. So there’s no reason for Democrats in Congress to play that game unless and until it suits their broader aims in particular circumstances. Pick your spots.That still leaves a lot of room for congressional oversight that can have real impact, and there are some signs that Democrats get this. A sample, non-comprehensive list includes:: A premium source of unsanctioned disclosures for congressional investigators will be whistleblowers inside and outside of government. It will includes current government employees, former government officials in the first two years of Trump II, and federal contractors and grant recipients. All of these categories of whistleblowers have protections under the law for divulging corruption and wrongdoing, including retaliation against them. They have first-hand accounts and in some instances documentary evidence that doesn’t need to be subpoenaed or otherwise pried loose from the administration.Government contractors and grant recipients: Congress can subpoena the companies, organizations, and other entities that the federal government does business with, thereby bypassing the administration. Congressional investigators have a potentially rich trove of documents and witnesses to mine here. The list is too long to do it justice, but to give you a sampling it includes everyone from defense contractors to NGOs crippled by the USAID cuts to construction companies working on Trump’s pet projects to ICE vendors. It includes not just prime contractors but subcontractors, suppliers, and vendors.: Congressional investigations can legitimately reach beyond the federal government and the companies that directly do business with it to those people and entities who have been targeted by the Trump administration, who have capitulated, and who have curried favor with it. This category is also too broad to fully list here but think along the lines of: the Big Law firms and media companies who negotiated settlements with Trump; the donors to the Trump ballroom project and the Trump library; the research centers where grants and funding have been cut or politicized or both; the universities ostensibly targeted for alleged anti-semitism or for allegedly continuing affirmative action in admissions; industries crippled by illegal tariffs, etc.It is, as the military would say, a target-rich environment. Democrats can make retribution, corruption, and destruction the storyline themselves or use those as the underpinnings for broader stories about affordability or whatever other line of attack they see as more accessible or voter-friendly.None of this is easy, but it’s all very doable, and they’re are plenty of signs that Democrats already recognize the opportunities here. One of the real advantages to controlling both chambers is the power of agenda-setting: You can pick which stories to tell and which not to. You have flexibility to pivot as new information emerges or as public sentiment coalesces or shifts.I wanted to frame this all up for you in part to set expectations. I wouldn’t be looking to the courts for salvation on congressional oversight, at least not in the next 18 months. I wouldn’t expect the Trump administration to do anything that even implicitly recognizes the legitimacy of the Democratic Congress. If you’re most desired endgame is Stephen Miller in tears at the witness table in an ornate Senate hearing room, let it go.The hard work of congressional oversight is mostly away from the cameras doing due diligence and painstakingly reviewing documents and databases. The magic — which few investigators and electeds have the skillsets to pull off — is in being able to convert that hard work into politically salient storylines that resonate in the public consciousness.It doesn’t necessarily have to be a Watergate or Jan. 6 hearing or other mega-scandal to break through. It can be done with less celebrated stories, and often it’s not the story you expected or foresaw. Facts are funny that way. They sometimes capture the public imagination in surprising and unanticipated ways.While it’s true that President Trump’s corrupt decimation of the Justice Department deprives congressional Democrats (and us all) of enforcement mechanisms for contempt of Congress and of criminal and civil accountability for wrongdoing, congressional oversight has not lost its salience.Perhaps the most powerful effect of congressional oversight is that it’s — to borrow another military phrase — a force multiplier. The fruits of congressional investigations combine with good journalism, ongoing legal proceedings, state and investigations to reinforce and buttress each other. Each can leverage the other to unearth new facts, puts those facts in proper context, and shine a concentrated light on wrongdoing and wrongdoers. It’s a powerful combination.Politico’s Alice Ollstein: Georgia, Kansas and Texas eye Medicaid expansion after midterms rompCornyn Signals Trouble For OLC HeadOutgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) is poised to sink President Trump’s judicial nomination of T. Elliot Gaiser — who as head of the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel has sanctioned some of the worst depredations of the Trump II presidency.Gaiser’s confirmation hearing was set for this morning, but Cornyn signaled yesterday that he may not yield on the Gaiser nomination to a federal judgeship in Texas.Under the Senate’s blue-slip tradition, Cornyn’s approval would be typically be required to move the nomination. Gaiser, an Ohion native, has very limited connections to Texas and was not on the short list that the two Texas senators sent to the White House.For the second time this year, President Trump told a Black female journalist that she doesn’t “see dirt.”Trump’s comments yesterday came in response to a question from NBC White House correspondent Yamiche Alcindor, who is Black:Back in May, Trump made a virtually identical comment in response to a question from ABC News senior political correspondent Rachel Scott, who is also Black. “You probably don’t see dirt,” he said, gesturing to Scott. “But I do.”‘I Believe That It’s the SI’

item.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to :Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL scriptSelect a released version of Datasette to load from PyPILoad a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repositoryPick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with DatasetteInstall additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization toolsThe ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.As an example, consider the following URL:Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this:That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing:https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass as many times as you like to load more plugins. loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending fragment hash to it ( is a URL-encoded ) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the column in the data.I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:How this works, using service workersDatasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.The problem with that initial version is that it was a . It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using .This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS) Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a prefix. What's that about?The prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.The service worker for is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production!Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLiteDatasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process.WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whlThat's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.Datasette Lite now takes a special URL parameter, which will accept a version number like , resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.This should work for every other Python app, tooNothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026.One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.

item.title: Lakes Are Bizarrely Syncing Up Globally, And Scientists Are Worried
item.author: Becky Ferreira
item.content:encoded: Lakes around the world have become increasingly synced up in their ecological conditions—such as warming temperatures, algal blooms, and oxygen levels—a trend that reveals “a possible fundamental reorganization of the world’s lake systems,” according to a study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Lakes come in all kinds of shapes, sizes, and volumes, and vary widely in other critical properties, such as temperature, composition, and biomass. This diversity of lake conditions, known as spatial heterogeneity, serves as a handy buffer against environmental disruptions; because each lake responds to events differently, they curb the spread of potential damage.But when scientists studied satellite imagery of roughly 2,000 lakes around the world since the year 2000, they discovered that lakes “are undergoing a profound shift toward spatial synchrony through time” that “strongly indicates that increasing lake synchrony is a genuine, global-scale phenomenon,“ according to the study.“Lakes, although covering less than 2 percent of Earth’s surface, play disproportionate roles in regulating global biogeochemical cycles and macroscale ecological dynamics,” said researchers led by Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. “They bury carbon at rates far exceeding those of the oceans, store roughly half as much organic carbon as terrestrial soils, emit greenhouse gases equivalent to ~20 percent of fossil fuel emissions, recycle nutrients that structure regional and global biogeochemical cycles, and sustain exceptional levels of biodiversity. Lakes are also critically important social–ecological systems, providing vital ecosystem services for billions.”Yet despite the important role they play in supporting life and modulating the climate, lakes are typically managed on local or regional levels. This approach will have to change as lakes approach global synchrony, rendering them more vulnerable to heatwaves, droughts, and the encroachment of urban development, all of which contribute to the phenomenon, according to the study.“Coincident algal blooms or hypoxia events could trigger parallel lake ecosystem collapses across continents, eroding the regional diversity essential for ecosystem recovery and adaptation,” Zhang’s team said in the study. “In effect, increasing synchrony erodes the spatial asynchrony that once buffered local disturbances, indicating a shift toward geographically widespread ecological responses to shared global pressures.”Zhang and his colleagues were able to confirm the increase in synchrony across three datasets: satellite-derived chlorophyll levels, water transparency in thousands of lakes, and sedimentary records from 119 lakes spanning the past century. The results suggest that lakes are no longer a varied patchwork of environments, but an increasingly interwoven system that must be addressed on national and global levels.“The emerging evidence for increasing global lake synchrony calls for a conceptual shift: lake ecosystems can no longer be viewed as isolated systems experiencing local degradation, but should also be recognized as sensitive indicators of increasingly coupled environmental pressures,” the researchers said.“Our findings support this hypothesis and indicate that the synchronized, planetary-scale behaviors of lakes are an emergent property of the Anthropocene,” the team concluded.

item.title: Emails Show Administrators Seeking To Have Protections For Non-Revenue Sports Stripped From PCSA
item.author: Jon Loesche
item.content:encoded: On July 10, University of Oklahoma President Joseph Harroz Jr. emailed Southeastern Conference Commissioner Greg Sankey and leaders of the other 15 SEC universities, urging the conference to prioritize stripping protections for Olympic sports from the Protect College Sports Act. “The current restrictions on Olympic sport sponsorship, funding, and scheduling should be removed,” Harroz wrote. Schools needed flexibility to “respond to consumer demand.”If the conference could not resolve the issues together, Harroz said he would address them “from Oklahoma’s perspective.” Action was necessary, he warned, as schools should expect “another unbudgeted increase of $10+ million” in football roster costs next year.University of Mississippi Chancellor Glenn Boyce responded the next day, saying he agreed with Harroz.

item.title: Racist with shitty hair does a racism, to the surprise of nobody
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Hey, let’s check in with that racist slumlord from Queens, New York. You know who I mean. The one who, in 1973, along with his tyrant Klansman father, got fined by the federal government for refusing to rent any of their shitty apartments to black people.What ever happened to that guy? NBC News White House correspondent Yamiche Alcindor: “What do you say to critics who say you were too focused on DC construction projects while our airline systems were crumbling, given the fact that Republicans have been in control?”Racist slumlord from Queens: “Well, if you take a look at the White House, it’s flawless. If you— listen to me, I know you don’t see dirt, but if you take a look at the White House, you never notice broken windows, obviously, from where you come.”‘From where you come’? What the fuck? Yamiche Alcindor was born and raised in Miami. I guess when the racist slumlord from Queens sees someone with black skin, he just presumes they’re from one of what he so charmingly calls the ‘shithole’ countries.Okay, I have an idea. Hear me out. You know that Arlington Guard who became a national hero last week for screaming ‘ALL VISITORS WILL MAINTAIN AN ATMOSPHERE OF SILENCE AND PAY RESPECT!’ at Piss-Drunk Pete and his giggling entourage?You know you I’m talking about. This dude. Can we get that Guard to stand right behind Donny and scream something like ‘ALL PRESIDENTS WILL STOP BEING A RACIST FUCKING MORON!” every time he opens his damn fool mouth?So this is now a thing, with Donny? His dementia has increased to the point where all filters have gone , and he’ll just be as racist as he wants to be? Remember, it was just last week that he spewed pretty much the same bigoted crap about Obama, during one of his Oval Bordello whine sessions.“When you look at that White House, you know, I hear Obama, but he— Obama doesn’t know about dirt and filth. And he doesn’t know about cracked stones. And he doesn’t know about broken windows. He’s probably fine with them. But I’m not. I’m not fine with them.”So, inside the putrefying pudding-brain of the racist slumlord from Queens, black people have some kind of endemic filth-blindness. What a completely fucked-up thing to believe.You absolutely know who taught Donny to be this racist, don’t you? Of course you do. It was Donny’s own father — the one who got arrested at a Klan rally in 1927. You just know that at some point, Old Fred sat his son down and said, ‘now Donny, we don’t rent to black people. They’re animals. They don’t see dirt. They don’t care about broken windows.’Except the word he used probably didn’t start with B.This is what we’re dealing with. A president who imagines he’s superior to others, simply because of the color of his skin. And he’s aided and abetted by an undead Chief of Staff and a piss-drunk Secretary of Death who believe the same fucked-up thing.The racist slumlord from Queens has a lot of goddamned gall, looking down on Obama as an inferior. Have you ever seen those side-by-side photos of Donny and Obama with the Queen?Obama looks like an elegant world leader. Donny looks like the hungover waiter at a cut-rate strip-mall spaghetti restaurant.Oh, can we get that hero Guard back in here for a minute?Reporter: “Any update on what happened last Friday with the FAA and the airspace?” Donny: “I hate to blame anybody, but the Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass, and copper, if you know anything about electrical engineering, you cannot hook up copper into glass.”Oh dear sweet Confucius on a crab cake, he’s such a fucking idiot. If I had to guess, I’d say that someone tried to explain to Sundowning Grandpa Befuddlepants about converting copper wires to fiber optic cable — and the moron understood absolutely zero of what he was told. Only now, the racist slumlord imagines that he knows more about electrical engineering than all the electrical engineers — even the big, strong teary-eyed ones, like few thought possible. Listen to him blither about ‘copper into glass.’ He has no idea what he’s talking about, yet he’s supremely convinced of his own genius.Oh, to have the serene self-confidence of the mediocre white man. Donny is what would happen if Dunning and Kruger had a baby, and then repeatedly dropped it on its head.And guess what: you absolutely ‘hook up copper into glass.’ In the interest of Responsible Journalism and Everything™, I asked Google’s janky, six-fingered plagiarism robot exactly that, and here’s what it told me.You can interface copper wiring with fiber-optic (glass) cabling. This is a standard practice in modern data and telecommunication networks. [1, 2] Devices like , transceivers (such as SFP modules), or act as the bridge, translating electrical— Okay, you can shut the fuck up now, plagiarism robot. Let me stop you right there. We don’t need to know it works, just that it work.My god, how the plagiarism bot will natter on, if you let it.Reporter: “What responsibility do you take for the ground stop on Friday given that you're the president?”Donny: “I don’t take any responsibility.”Donny not taking responsibility? Gee, where have I heard this before? Of course Donny won’t take responsibility. That’s how chickenshit cowards roll, even though this whole mess is his fault. He’s the one who fired the team Biden had assembled to oversee the air traffic control upgrade. He’s the one who, on the first day of his second term, signed an executive order freezing the funds that had been allocated for the upgrade. He’s the only who let a reality-show wash-out be Transportation Secretary, and put a failed plumber’s assistant in charge of Homeland Security. He’s the only who didn’t raise a finger to stop the Space Nazi’s merry band of unfuckable DOGE incels from firing four hundred experts at the FAA. The racist slumlord from Queens , whether he wants to admit it or not.Oh, can we hear from our hero Guard one final time?‘ALL PRESIDENTS WILL STOP COMBING THEIR FUCKED-UP RAT’S NEST OF COTTON-CANDY BULLSHIT HAIR WITH AN EGG-BEATER!”Yeeesh. What the fuck is going on up there? I’ll bet the racist slumlord from Queens doesn’t take responsibility for the debacle on top of his big, dumb pumpkin head, either.Everything right now, and is going to continue to until at least January 3rd of next year, but at least we can enjoy these Rutgers students screaming ‘get the fuck out of here’ at the Itsy-Bitsy Nazi, Obergruppenführer Greg Bovino, until he flees the Rutgers Republicans event where he’d been trying to speak.Now let’s have us our Daily Claudia.Oh hey, I found some more wedding photos that I’d forgotten existed, while sorting though some of Ms Spouse’s files yesterday.You’ve seen this one before.But I’ve never posted these two, from September 4, 1984.Have a great Tuesday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: 'Defense by ChatGPT'
item.author: Samantha Cole
item.content:encoded: We've written a lot about how AI generated writing has collided with – and created chaos for – the legal system in the last few years, from lawyers using it to do their research and filings for them to judges getting extremely fed up with dealing with these attorneys. In some cases, judges have sanctioned offending attorneys thousands of dollars for using AI to do their jobs, and lawyers when they're busted, with some calling it ." Today's story is about how the DOJ is getting involved: by trying to catch attorneys doing "defense by ChatGPT." Lawyers for the Department of Justice are using the AI writing detection service Pangram to argue that opposing attorneys are using AI to write legal arguments, and in one case told the court that opposing counsel was doing “defense by ChatGPT,” and writing “AI slop” filings, according to court filings reviewed by 404 Media. Over the last few years, we have documented many attorneys getting caught by judges using AI after citing hallucinated cases that do not exist. The filings in this court case over the past month show attorneys, including those working for the government, are trying to catch each other using AI, then are citing their opponents’ AI use in their arguments to the court.“This case has turned into defense by ChatGPT,” government attorneys wrote in the case, which centers around a high-profile voter fraud case. “Motions practice in this case is the equivalent of writing responses to documents generated by a robot that is attempting to practice law. It cannot be that the local rules envisioned that it was acceptable for defense to use what the kids would call ‘AI slop’ to create multiple frivolous motions that waste judicial resources and fail to serve the cause of justice.”404 contributor Matthew Gault took the bullet for us all: “Three hours and 15 minutes into the four hour long documentary Musk, a video game avatar of the titular billionaire picks up a chainsaw off the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. Shot like a first-person shooter, the audience watches as Musk wields the chainsaw to destroy various government buildings. Walking through a farm, Musk aims the chainsaw at grain silos labeled ‘USDA’ and lightning arcs from its spinning blades. The silo explodes and cows moo in distress. In my experience, the purpose of a video game chainsaw is to viscerally rend through objects. I have never seen one shoot lightning. It’s a small detail that speaks to my overall problem with Alex Gibney’s Musk: it’s cringe.”“Public lands belong in public hands.” “A dozen Democrats in Washington are taking steps to either ban the construction of data centers on public lands or investigate whether the Trump administration stands to profit from infrastructure deals to support the AI industry.” A new study marking the first peer-reviewed estimates of the biggest US data center carbon dioxide emissions found that these campuses are “responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually — almost as much as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark,” the reports.Suddenly I’m into GTA VI. According to a reporter who got an advance walkthrough of , which comes out on Thursday, the game has 62 types of birds you can find and collect: “Later, I see a gull sitting on a post by the beach and ask, just to be annoying, what kind of bird it is. Jason pulls out a pair of binoculars, the gull is recorded in a wildlife logbook, and I am told with pride that there are 62 types of birds to spot.” If we get an OOO from you on Thursday, we all know what you’re up to.

item.title: The Department of Justice Is Using AI Detector Pangram Against Defense Attorneys
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: Lawyers for the Department of Justice are using the AI writing detection service Pangram to argue that opposing attorneys are using AI to write legal arguments, and in one case told the court that opposing counsel was doing “defense by ChatGPT,” and writing “AI slop” filings, according to court filings reviewed by 404 Media. Over the last few years, we have documented many attorneys getting caught by judges using AI after citing hallucinated cases that do not exist. The filings in this court case over the past month show attorneys, including those working for the government, are trying to catch each other using AI, then are citing their opponents’ AI use in their arguments to the court.“This case has turned into defense by ChatGPT,” government attorneys wrote in the case, which centers around a high-profile voter fraud case. “Motions practice in this case is the equivalent of writing responses to documents generated by a robot that is attempting to practice law. It cannot be that the local rules envisioned that it was acceptable for defense to use what the kids would call ‘AI slop’ to create multiple frivolous motions that waste judicial resources and fail to serve the cause of justice.”The defendant is Khalwinder Bhengura, an Indian man who entered the United States on an immigrant visa in 2022 and illegally — and apparently accidentally, according to his lawyers — registered to vote in Texas in 2024 after falsely stating that he was an American citizen on his application for a driver’s license. Bhengura was arrested in September on charges of lying about his citizenship status, illegally registering to vote, and illegally voting in the 2024 election, and was found guilty in October on two of the three counts. His family and lawyers have argued that the whole thing is a misunderstanding, and that Bhengura, who is 70 years old and does not speak English well, did not know he was committing a crime and did not understand what he was doing. Bhengura’s case is one of a few dozen in which the Trump administration found disparate cases of voter fraud (which is exceedingly rare) and made big, public shows of the arrests it made. Beyond the political implications of the case, the filings by the Department of Justice show that attorneys are now trying to catch each other using AI, and are centering some of their arguments to the judge around the idea that their opposition is wasting the court’s time with AI-generated filings. The case is taking place in federal court in the Northern District of Texas, which recently implemented a rule requiring attorneys to disclose generative AI use in filings. In some of the filings, Bhengura’s attorneys wrote “portions of this brief were prepared with the assistance of a generative artificial intelligence tool.” Government attorneys ran several of the filings through Pangram, the AI writing detection service, and filed the results as exhibits to one of its arguments. The Pangram results for the filings were mixed (as in, they did not show that the briefings were 100 percent AI-drafted), but the government’s attorneys wrote that they did not feel like they should have to respond substantively to briefs that were partially AI-generated.The United States has “been trying to economize the amount of effort it puts into responding to Defendant’s meritless motions given that Defendant appears to be almost entirely using AI to generate them,” the DOJ attorneys wrote.“As the Court can see from a cursory review of the results of Bhengura’s motions, most of the non-AI generated text in these filings consists of statements from third parties other than Defense counsel, including statements from evidence or documents in the record or quotes from caselaw. In other words, virtually nothing of substance in these filings seems to have been drafted by a human on the Defense team,” they added., Mark Pittman, chastised the defense attorneys for their use of AI, and wrote, “This Court is disturbed by counsel’s repeated filings which subtly bend the law by proffering superficially persuasive but fundamentally meritless arguments so clearly generated by artificial intelligence. Defendant is not a pro se litigant; he has three counsel of record with decades of practice between them. It is distressing to see how quickly the advent of artificial intelligence has undermined counsels’ ability to properly advocate for their client.”Nicole Knox and Mario Herrera, two of Bhengura’s attorneys, told 404 Media that the story isn’t so simple, and say they felt they had to use AI because of a health emergency and in order to meet the court’s tight filing deadlines ahead of the election. Herrera said Knox “experienced a medical emergency while we were at the U.S. Attorney's Office preparing the case with the prosecutors […] thus, I prepared a federal jury trial in four days with the lead attorney in the hospital.”“I represented my client to the best of my abilities within this limited timeframe. I utilized all available legal tools and did not violate any rules or laws in doing so,” he said. “The government's ‘evidence’ consisted of output from Pangram, an AI-detection software. An AI-detection software identifies patterns in writing styles based upon a document’s content. It cannot determine who wrote a document, how it was written, or if the law applied within a document is correct,” Herrera added. “The U.S. Attorney's Office did not identify any false citations. ‘Defense by ChatGPT’ is a label the government placed in a court filing regarding the defense of a 70-year-old permanent resident facing prison and deportation. It is not a factual statement. And the attorneys who wrote it were present when Ms. Knox collapsed. They knew precisely why I was standing alone with a new co-counsel in that courtroom four days later. There was nothing requiring them to state what they stated.” Pangram CEO Max Spero told 404 Media that anecdotally, he has heard that law firms have begun to use his company’s software, but that most use cases he has seen have been from firms using the tool internally to check whether their junior attorneys and paralegals are using AI to draft legal briefs. Herrera said that the fact that Bhengura was found not guilty on one of the three counts he faced is evidence that “Mr. Bhengura received the representation that he deserved.”“Lawyers have been using templates, forms, and drafting software for decades. This is merely a newer version of those very tools. The arguments that the judge attacked were written by me. Some portions of the filings were written with the aid of AI but then reviewed and edited by me. All final work product was mine and I stand behind the argument and logic of each and every document,” he added. “It was the use of AI during that week that allowed me to work on many tasks at once and produce so much work in four days.” Knox added, “AI could have never come up with our argument,” and said that the new AI disclosure rule has made it such that “if you obtain one sentence or phrase through the use of A.I., then you must disclose it. We have nothing to hide.”“Mr. Bhengura is 70 years old, a lawful permanent resident of this country, speaks Punjabi, and his English is limited. Our defense on the one count of which the jury acquitted him was that he never knowingly claimed to be a U.S. citizen,” Herrera said. “He has been in custody since the verdict, and in addition to whatever sentence he receives for the offenses of which he has been found guilty, he faces deportation from this country. He is entitled to more compassion and humanity from everyone involved in this case than he has received so far.”The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Religious freedom takes courage
item.author: 010001a1ea096457-40fc6583-167b-4d23-9b61-3b00287c8def-000000@amazonses.com
item.content:encoded: In Texas and across the country, AU and our allies are challenging laws that force public schools to display the Ten Commandments. We’re working alongside the families affected by these laws, bringing decades of legal experience to these cases, and asking the U.S. Supreme Court to hear our argument that public schools should welcome every student, regardless of what they believe.That’s what meeting this moment requires: people coming together and being willing to act.As Legal Director, I can tell you that Americans United is at the heart of that work. Our legal team is prepared to challenge these laws whenever they threaten religious freedom, but we can’t do it without your support.

item.title: Wasting Time
item.content:encoded: I saw this on one of the social sites the other day, but I can’t remember which (or who shared it)…“Wasting time” might be one of the strangest accusations we’ve ever invented. Apparently you can waste 2:00 p.m. by sitting under a tree doing nothing.The afternoon was going to pass either way. The Earth was going to rotate either way. But because you didn’t convert those hours into money, errands or improvement, we decided the time itself was wasted.As if simply being alive isn’t enough to justify an afternoon.

item.title: The AI in ‘Musk’ Is Cringe
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: Three hours and 15 minutes into the 4 hour long documentary a video game avatar of the titular billionaire picks up a chainsaw off the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. Shot like a first-person shooter, the audience watches as Musk wields the chainsaw to destroy various government buildings. Walking through a farm, Musk aims the chainsaw at grain silos labeled ‘USDA’ and lightning arcs from its spinning blades. The silo explodes and cows moo in distress.In my experience, the purpose of a video game chainsaw is to viscerally rend through objects. I have never seen one shoot lightning. It’s a small detail that speaks to my overall problem with Alex Gibney’s : it’s cringe.Elon Musk is one of the most powerful men alive on the planet and Gibney’s does a decent job of giving the overall arc of the man’s many faults. The director takes us from Zip2 to DOGE while highlighting the billionaire’s pathology, and it hits more than it misses. is a good overview of the general arc of Elon Musk, the man. But there have been other Elon Musk documentaries told in much the same way ( several years ago, that is similar in tone and vibe). And so, at a laborious four hours long, it’s not clear who is for, and the weird video game interstitials and ghoulish AI avatar of Musk himself are genuinely distracting. Musk would not talk to Gibney so the director generated an AI avatar of the billionaire to act as a stand-in. Throughout , this hyperreal grotesque lends color commentary as if the billionaire is actually in the room.The director cites Musk’s oft-stated belief that we’re living in a simulation as a justification for the AI Musk. “He believed it likely that an artificial intelligence of the future had exfiltrated all knowledge and life experiences from planet Earth and was now running an ancestor simulation in which our past lives had become the training data for a kind of sim world,” Gibney says as the AI musk coalesces before the audience. “In honor of that idea, we decided to edit together recordings of his actual words to create a simulated interview at the heart of a kind of documentary video game.I understand what is going for here, and it’s funny to watch Musk’s likeness and spirit rendered through the lens of AI and video games. But, on the whole, the AI Elon doesn’t work. Its head is too big, its features are exaggerated, and it sits in a stereotypical gamer chair while bathed in the kind of blue and red lighting popular on Twitch streams ten years ago. The things the bot says aren’t fabricated, they’re direct quotes from the man himself, though some are lightly edited.In every instance, the quotes are more interesting and more informative when shown in their actual context, in the video interviews the real Musk gave.“I lost my son, essentially. They call it dead naming because, uh, your son is dead. So my son is dead. Killed by the woke mind virus,” AI Elon says in the film.This was part of an interview with Jordan Peterson for The Daily Wire. Learning that enriches the quote. There’s crosstalk with Peterson. You see Musk’s real face when he talks about Vivian. It is a real video interview that you can actually watch. There is no need to use an AI avatar to do this.In another clip the AI Elon explains the Twitter Files. “On Twitter, there was a lot of censorship. We sort of uncovered a lot of that with the Twitter Files,” it says. “Free speech is meaningless unless you allow people you don’t like to say things you don’t like.” The real clip comes from a Real Time With Bill Maher interview.There’s a lot of this in the film. “What is the most entertaining outcome for the election? That’s probably what’s going to happen,” the Musk bot grins evilly while a . Musk talking to Kara Swisher, Musk at a Vanity Fair conference, Musk delivering missives at CPAC, and Musk speaking to Joe Rogan are all condensed into an AI approximation of the real person. In every instance, the original quote in its context is more powerful and more illuminating about its subject.And then there’s the video game sequences. uses Elon’s obsession with video games as an extended visual metaphor throughout. Under a pink filter that looks like it’s designed to capitalize on the release of , Musk picks different classes — shifting from gamer to founder to Kublai Khan. He drives a sports car along a digital track while Tesla’s stock pieces rises like a video game score, and uses Iron Man-style gloves to vaporize Twitter employees.If the man believes we’re living in a video game then this is what it might look like. His DOGE -fueled chainsaw rampage across DC ends with him dropping a nuke on the National Nuclear Safety Administration and his inauguration Nazi salute turned into a pixel-art version score screen.Again, this is a four-hour long documentary. It has an intermission, even when you stream it. The video game sequences and AI Elon feel like a baby boomer grasping the aesthetics of a younger generation and misusing them. It’s Steve Buscemi holding a skateboard in the hallway of a high school asking how his fellow kids are doing. It detracts from the overall message here, which is that Musk is a destructive force in our businesses and politics.After publication, public relations team reached out to 404 Media to say, “The Musk avatar was made with CGI and was hand-designed, AI was only used to sync the sound to the image they created," a representative from Falco Ink told 404 Media.In multiple interviews about , Gibney himself calls the avatar AI. “You need to embrace the air of unreality in order to bring a sense of reality to bear. You have to explore the tools of deception and manipulation to get out the other side. That’s why we came up with the AI avatar of Elon Musk,” Gibney told the International Documentary Association.“The AI elements that we used were really to get the sync, and even that was interesting [...] we were using an AI artist at Makemake and very much using the tools to try to refine stuff. But it wasn’t like generative AI where you press a button and suddenly this slop appears,” Gibney told Edward Niedermeyer in an interview. “We gave it a lot of consideration.” This piece has been updated with a statement from ’s public relations team and more context from comments Gibney has made.

item.title: Voyager 1, A Day Of Light Away
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: Humans have trouble with inhuman distances. Miles are about the largest comprehensible unit of measurement we have, because we can understand miles. Watering hole is in a mile? No problem, we’ll be there soon. Aurochs herd is 30 miles away? OK, our hunting party won't walk that in a day, but it’s doable. Miles are a good measure for us, and on the scale of the universe, absolutely useless.The Sun is about 93 million miles from Earth. Can that possibly be spatially encompassed by a human mind that evolved to think in terms of footsteps? The nearest star after that is about 25 trillion miles away. We have the words, but they blur into a meaningless litany of zeroes and -illions. How big is the observable universe? 546,710,000,000,000,000,000,000 miles across, best we can tell. What does that mean to us? Nothing. I submit that while it’s less accurate, it’s more truthful to say simply that the universe is “very big.”Enter light. The fastest thing there is, light travels through a vacuum at 186,000 miles per second, which gives us a helpful benchmark for talking about cosmic distances. (And, in a universe where everything is flying around in different directions, light travels at the same speed from any reference point, which is not intuitive but very helpful. Good job, Einstein.) So 186,000 miles is called a light-second. A light-year, naturally, is the distance it takes light to travel in a year. We can say that Proxima Centauri, alluded to in the previous paragraph, is 25 trillion miles away, or we can say that it’s about four light-years away. Guess which astronomers prefer.

item.title: How to Fix Our Attention Spans
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Much has been written about our shrinking attention spans in the last couple of decades, which coincidentally exploded with the introduction of smart phones and social media. Those accounts are mostly complaints instead of serious discussions of causes and remedies. You mostly notice shortened attention spans in other people, but if you are honest, it probably affects you, too. The reason is that there are more attractive distractions than ever before. We are primed to notice things, but once upon a time, there wasn't so much to notice all at once. This TED-Ed lesson explains how distractibility is normal and natural, and trying to focus in a distracting environment is hard. But it's worth working on for yourself. (via Laughing Squid)

item.title: None of This Computes
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: The new meaning of Singularity is when only one of your tech services is still working. It’s been a rough week in tech, and I’m not talking about Jensen Huang’s seven-year itch glitch. For a warm-up, Microsoft had a massive outage that made email inaccessible for millions. Then there was that little router upgrade in Arkansas that grounded planes across the country. People were finally able to fly home, only to realize that they were temporarily unable to access their bank accounts. Today, Apple has confirmed an iCloud outage, affecting Apple Pay and other services. All of these issues, we’ve been told, have been due to unrelated software bugs or bad updates. But we’re all so dependent on technology, it’s hard not to worry that something more nefarious is afoot. Even harder when the week of crazy tech headlines has led to this one from CNN: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down, sources say. I’m hoping the timing of all these snafus is just a weird coincidence. But I’m still considering this to be a tech apocalypse level Defcon 3. (Defcon 1 is when Netflix stops streaming.)+ Luckily, we have just the leadership in place to manage these issues and give us assurances we can trust. “President Donald Trump brushed off recent mass outages that wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails … ‘It’s life, it’s life … ‘When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.'” OK, now may be a good time to back up your data … and your democracy. (I wonder if the nation’s technology stack can be rebooted by someone with bone spurs in his foot?)My son was born around the time the first iPhone was released, so he’s really never had my full attention. Of course, he’s also never had full attention. I doubt he, or anyone else, will be surprised that the latest data indicates the school phone bans around the country are gradually leading to improved test scores. “Schools with strict bans — requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day — saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found.” I’m not sure that positioning these results as being the equivalent of more school is the best way to get buy-in from young people, but we all know that it’s better to put your phone in a locker than to check your brain at the door. But what if turning off technology required doing the latter? The interface between the brain and computing is the next frontier, and like many new technologies, the possibilities are both breathtakingly awesome and incredibly disturbing. J. Galen Buckwalter has already had experiences across the spectrum. He regularly allows “a researcher to attach wires to three metal knobs screwed into his skull like a cyberpunk mohawk. The wires connect to six chips that were implanted in his brain during a seven-hour craniotomy. They record his neural signals — the firing of his brain when he thinks, speaks or moves — and transmit them to a computer to be analyzed.” He’s hoping the technology can be of assistance to him (he’s almost totally paralyzed) and others: “Brain-computer interfaces have enabled people with paralysis to fly drones and helped people who have lost the ability to speak to communicate — using just their thoughts. Eventually, researchers say, they could allow the regulation of emotions such as pain or fear; the instant transfer of knowledge, such as a new language; or the merging of human consciousness with artificial intelligence.” (That escalated quickly.) Buckwalter has also learned that some of the same data handling issues that have come up on the internet are now coming up in his brain, as data ownership of your gray matter is a particularly gray area. (Gift Article): Does This Man Have a Right to the Data From His Own Brain? What do you think about all this? Actually, don’t tell me. We’ll find out soon enough.“China is the principal backer of Russia’s war against Ukraine, providing essential supplies that keep Moscow’s missiles and drones flying. Russia is giving Iran satellite imaging and overhead targeting data even as Iran strikes U.S. military assets in the Gulf region. Chinese companies have provided Iran with crucial missile components. Joint Chinese and Russian military exercises in the western Pacific are increasingly active around Japan and near contested island territories. Beneath the appearance of accord at the trilateral summit, Mr. Trump will be making nice with opponents who have daggers drawn against our allies and partners in three of the world’s most dangerous spots.” So you get it, right? These are not our allies. But not everyone gets it. (Gift Article): Trump’s Ego Trip With Xi and Putin Will End Badly. (On the plus side, Trump’s Asia trip got off to a spirited start in Manila, where he was greeted with a rousing rendition of YMCA. We’ve never been so respected!)+ To the extent there are any serious negotiations at this summit, they might be between factions inside the Trump administration. (Gift Article): Trump Administration Divide on China Policy Breaks Into Public View. (It can be broken down as a battle between those who want to partially sell out American interests for personal gain and to appease the president, and those who want to fully sell out American interests for the same reasons.) “Amid the fallout, Mr. Trump has appeared more concerned in public about offending Mr. Xi than about the risks to national security.”Jensen Huang has agreed to talk with House lawmakers trying to get to the bottom of exactly how much Nvidia shared with, and sold to, China. He’s also agreed to come back as CEO if you really, really want him to. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” (It’s this kind of smooth, sweet-talking that got him into this mess in the first place.)+ “The records illustrate that the couple operated on both sides of the U.S.-China technology divide: Chinese state money was invested in Kang’s domestic ventures as his wife’s overseas company gained access to the chips Washington was trying to keep out of China. Kang connected those worlds, having known Jensen Huang from both men’s days in the videogame industry. Kang told people who know the couple that he had introduced his wife to Jensen and that he appeared to accept their romantic relationship.” (Gift Article): Alice Huang’s Husband Built a Data-Center Empire Backed by the Chinese State. “New US intelligence indicates that Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC, even as officials continue to debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute such a plot.” (Is the leak of this information more reality, politics, or strategy? All answers are worrisome, some more than others.)+ Troubled Bridge Over Water: “Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an ‘unprecedented’ military operation.”+ “I found no hidden explanation for what had happened to him. As best as I could establish, Sanchez is set to spend the next 30 years in prison simply for moving a box of radical zines.” (Gift Article): 30 Years for Moving a Box.+ “To commemorate The New York Times’s 175th anniversary, The New York Times Magazine set for itself an impossible project: to select the 10 most consequential days since the paper began publishing.” Ten Days That Changed the World. (About 15 years ago, five or so folks from the NYT came to my office in SF to get my advice about their newsletter strategy. Not sure how that meeting didn’t make this list…)+ “Kelsey Rogers, a 26-year-old working in construction in San Antonio, Texas, didn’t want to tell her boss why she was asking for time off … She didn’t have to worry: Her boss admitted that he was taking time off for the same reason. ‘I don’t think the company’s even going to be up and running for probably two or three days,’ Rogers told me. If you’ve got a metal roof that needs replacing in south-central Texas, it just might have to wait.” The release of the new Grand Theft Auto game could result in The Least Productive Day of the Year.

item.title: 8Ball & MJG – On The Outside Looking In
item.author: deedub77
item.content:encoded: On their 1993 debut album (which, at nine tracks, felt more like an EP), 8Ball & MJG made quite an impression. The duo used their debut (and the Suave House label’s inaugural album) to spew brash bars filled with gangsta/player/pimp Memphis theology over Tony Draper’s lo-fi but funky production. The shit was pretty damn entertaining and more than lived up to its name. 8Ball & MJG would return in ‘94, looking to build on their debut’s momentum with their sophomore effort, .The founder and CEO of Suave House, Tony Draper, was credited with producing all of . For , 8Ball & MJG, along with South O, are credited with the production. track count is lengthier than ‘s, coming in at a healthy fifteen, and the duo invited a few guests to join them on a couple of records. is the first of two 8Ball & MJG albums distributed by Relativity Records. But even with Relativity’s support, the album failed to reach gold status (unlike the unofficial hood gold certification received).Hey. Some of my favorite hip-hop albums don’t have a gold certification. I’m still excited to look into this album from the outside. – Over slick background music suitable for a pimp’s conversation, 8Ball & MJG casually talk on the phone about finishing the album. It wasn’t a necessary intro, but I’ve heard far more useless ones. – The team creates a dark and mystic atmosphere (I’m pretty sure I hear sprinkled elements of “Nautilus” in the track) for 8Ball and MJG to grip their nuts and talk their gangsta shit, and the duo sounds convincing. Papa Reu stops by to add a little raspy dancehall chant to the hook, making the opening record sound even more menacing. – Slick, slippery production (complete with irresistible, whiny West Coast synth chords) that the Memphis duo slides all over, especially 8Ball. This track is complete flames. Easily one of my favorite records on the album. – Single-handedly, Dr. Dre has sampled “(Not Just) Knee Deep” and “Atomic Dog” enough to satisfy hip-hop’s eternal quota, even before 1994. So you can only imagine how excited I was to hear 8Ball & MJG spit generic party rhymes over unimaginative flips of both loops. This is the first dud on . – Now that’s a convoluted song title for a weed record. The late MC Breed joins our hosts as the trio transforms into the Sesshead Funk Brothers (according to MJG) and raps about their collective love for Mary Jane over obscure seventies funk. This was a fun, funky, feel-good record. But I’m sure Snoop wouldn’t agree with 8Ball’s claims of being the god of smoke or the almighty chiefa.– The backdrop features “Inner City Blues”-like instrumentation over Fred Wesley drums, while Rodney Ellis does his best Marvin Gaye impersonation on the hook. 8 & M get a little introspective as they discuss maintaining, despite living in a crooked system designed to make them fail. 8Ball’s depthful first verse might be the best one spat on the entire album. – Sticking with the Marvin Gaye theme, this sleek instrumental borrows from Marvin Gaye’s “I Want You.” 8 and M vow to stay ten toes down in the booth, streets, and life in general. This was tough; easily one of the best records on the album. – The song title might lead you to believe our hosts are going to share a day in the life of 8Ball & MJG. Instead, they reminisce about their childhood, early street hustles, and getting into the rap game. The rhymes were solid, but Rick James’ “Mary Jane” is another sample that should be hung in the hip-hop rafters and never used for anotha hip-hop song. – 8Ball gets the first solo joint of the evening. He spits a “true tale” that also works as a PSA about the consequences of living a life of crime, which he sums up as a “one-way road” to prison. Rapping from the criminal’s perspective keeps 8 from sounding preachy, and the solemn interpolated pieces from Isaac Hayes’ classic “Walk On By” give his one-verse wonder more validity.On Tha Outside Lookin’ In – The title track is a two-minute, one-verse MJG solo record, rapped from the perspective of an incarcerated hustler. It’s decent, but why the hell did they spell the album title correctly and the song title Ebonically? It might be a small discrepancy to you, but I find the inconsistency annoying as shit. – Well, they almost made it through an entire album without a misogyny track. But compared to the egregiousness of “Pimps” and “Niggas Like Us” on (which found 8Ball obsessed with “beatin’ up bitches”), this one almost feels wholesome. 8Ball made me chuckle a few times during the track, but overall, I wasn’t entertained. – Our hosts invite a few friends (Thorough and Crime Boss) to join them for this album-closing cipher session. Some Memphis hip-hop historians call this record a foundational piece of the Crunk movement that consumed hip-hop in the late nineties to early 2000s, mainly for its high-energy hook. I can rock with that theory.On “No Sellout,” 8Ball raps, “In ‘93 I was rappin’ about my curls and my Cadillac, the pimp blast, takin’ you fast, smokin’ grass and all that.” He follows those bars with “Players got the message, busters didn’t attempt to listen, thinkin’ that we was talkin’ about that on the-corner-fake-pimpin’.” Well, I beg your pardon, Mr. Ball, but I won’t allow you to insult my intelligence. I did listen to (which was released in ’93), from beginning to end several times over. You and MJG were clearly rapping about that “on-the-corner-fake-pimpin'” amongst other ignorant hood shit during the album’s nine-track runtime. The project was riddled with stories of violence, crime, and pimpin’, and all of the content was blunt and direct (sometimes uncomfortably blunt and direct) with no room left for abstract interpretation. I still enjoyed it, though. But I also enjoy seeing rappers show growth, which is what 8Ball & MJG do on On The Outside Looking In.8Ball and MJG don’t completely abandon the ratchetness that flooded . The misogyny is significantly toned down and approached more playfully on tracks like “Players Night Out” and “Break-A-Bitch College,” compared to the harsh tone of “Pimps” and “Niggas Like Us.” They provide a decent amount of tough guy talk (see “Lick ‘Em Up Shot,” “Crumbz 2 Brixx,” and “Lay It Down”), but tracks like “So What U Sayin’,” “No Sellout,” and “No Mercy” bring a level of consciousness to that didn’t exist on . It’s not Public Enemy or Boogie Down Productions levels of consciousness, but enough consciousness to bring a righteous balance to the album’s ratchetness. And while we’re speaking of balance, 8Ball and MJG may have been equally yoked lyrically on , but 8Ball is noticeably nicer with the bars than his counterpart on . As I mentioned at the beginning of this post, the Tony Draper-orchestrated production on had a low-budget feel. But the economical sonics felt soulful and kept my head bobbin’ for the most part. The instrumentals on are cleaner, crisper, and more developed than its predecessor; so what production lacks in soul, it compensates for with quality.The American businessman/poet Samuel Ullman once said: “Maturity is the ability to think, speak, and act your feelings within the bounds of dignity.” I may have enjoyed a little bit more than for the organically raw feel of the production. But their sophomore effort is a more dignified musical expression and a solid second outing from the Memphis tandem. -DeedubFollow me on Instagram @damontimeisillmatic
