item.title: From Rochester to Atlanta to Wilkes-Barre to Mohegan Sun: The Vacation That Forgot Where It Was Going
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: There are plenty of things that can go wrong when traveling. Flights get delayed, luggage gets lost, hotels turn out to be considerably less impressive than their photographs, and occasionally you end up spending $20 on a restaurant meal that tastes like something you could have purchased in the frozen-food section of a grocery store. Those things happen. They’re part of traveling.But there are certain travel experiences that are so ridiculous that they deserve to be remembered for years. Being forced to land in a city you never intended to visit, having no convenient way to get out, struggling to find food, discovering that there is practically nothing to do on a Saturday night, and eventually considering just about any transportation option that might get you somewhere else certainly qualifies.Our original plan was simple: travel from Rochester, New York, to Atlanta, Georgia. That was the destination. Atlanta was where we were supposed to be going, and Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, wasn’t even remotely part of the itinerary. We weren’t looking for a Pennsylvania vacation, weren’t researching hotels in northeastern Pennsylvania, and certainly weren’t trying to find the best Italian restaurant in Wilkes-Barre.We had no reason to be there.Then the FAA entered the picture.For reasons that resulted in us having to land, the aircraft was grounded in Wilkes-Barre. Just like that, our trip took an entirely different direction. We went from traveling toward Atlanta to being stuck in a Pennsylvania city that we had never intended to visit in the first place.There is something particularly frustrating about being stranded somewhere you didn’t choose. If you book a vacation and decide to visit a particular city, you generally have some idea of what you’re getting into. You research hotels, look at restaurants, find attractions, and make plans. Even if the destination isn’t everything you hoped it would be, at least you chose to go there.We didn’t choose Wilkes-Barre.The FAA essentially made that decision for us.And while the original circumstances of the grounding were beyond our control, everything that followed seemed to involve another unnecessary complication. Transportation became a problem. We had to share a car with a completely random dude just to get to the Holiday Inn. Once there, we discovered that finding food wasn’t particularly convenient. There was practically nothing nearby, DoorDash wasn’t much help, and eventually we had to walk approximately a mile to find an Italian restaurant.That restaurant turned out to be a disappointment of almost historic proportions. For approximately $20, we received something that was essentially a Lean Cuisine dinner. After walking a mile to get there, we might as well have gone to a grocery store, purchased a frozen meal, and heated it up in the hotel room.Saturday night wasn’t any better. We desperately tried to find something to do, but there was absolutely nothing that appealed to us. We searched for entertainment, considered possibilities, and eventually surrendered to watching the Sharter Show because apparently that was the best Wilkes-Barre had to offer.We even explored just about every possible way of getting out of town, including the possibility of taking a bus with a bunch of older passengers. When you’re considering transportation options you might never have entertained under normal circumstances simply because you want to escape your current location, you know the situation has become ridiculous.Somehow, though, there were a few unexpected bright spots. We managed to catch Arrested Development, which was a pretty good surprise considering the circumstances. And while Wilkes-Barre was doing its best to make us regret ever having heard of the place, we eventually managed to turn the situation into a collection of stories that would be considerably funnier in retrospect than they were while we were living through them.This wasn’t a planned vacation. It wasn’t a sightseeing adventure. It wasn’t some elaborate trip through Pennsylvania.It was a trip from Rochester to Atlanta that got hijacked by circumstances beyond our control.And Wilkes-Barre was where the adventure went off the rails.The Original Plan: Getting from Rochester to AtlantaThe journey began with a destination in mind and absolutely no expectation that Wilkes-Barre would become part of the story.Rochester to Atlanta. That was the plan.There was no reason to think we would end up spending an extended amount of time in northeastern Pennsylvania. We weren’t looking for somewhere to spend a weekend, and we certainly weren’t searching for recommendations about where to eat in Wilkes-Barre.Atlanta was the destination. Everything else was supposed to be part of getting there.That’s generally how traveling works. You make arrangements, figure out how you’re getting where you need to go, and expect that the transportation system will get you reasonably close to the intended destination. There might be a delay or an inconvenience, but you don’t generally expect to be deposited in an entirely different city and then have to figure out what happens next.Unfortunately, that is exactly what happened.The FAA forced the aircraft to land in Wilkes-Barre, and suddenly our original itinerary was meaningless.There is a difference between choosing to make an unexpected stop and having one imposed on you. If you’re driving and see an interesting town, you can decide to pull over, explore, get something to eat, and continue when you’re ready. That’s part of the fun of traveling.Being forced to land somewhere is a completely different experience.You aren’t stopping because you discovered a wonderful attraction. You aren’t stopping because somebody recommended an amazing restaurant. You aren’t stopping because you decided that the town looked interesting.You’re stopping because you have to.And when you find yourself in a city you never intended to visit, the first question is generally not, “What exciting attractions are available?”It’s, “How do we get out of here?”That became the central theme of the entire experience.We had gone from having a straightforward destination to having no particularly clear idea what the next steps would be. We needed somewhere to stay, transportation to that location, food, and eventually some way to continue moving toward where we originally intended to go.None of those things sounded especially complicated individually.Together, however, they would become an unexpectedly entertaining collection of travel disasters.There are plenty of reasons people end up making unexpected stops while traveling, but getting grounded by the FAA is certainly not something you put on your vacation checklist.You can prepare for a lot of things. You can bring extra clothes, make sure your phone is charged, keep some money available, and research alternate transportation. But you don’t necessarily expect that a trip from Rochester to Atlanta will suddenly involve an unplanned landing in Wilkes-Barre.The problem with an unexpected landing is that it doesn’t automatically solve anything beyond getting you on the ground.You still have to figure out where you’re going to stay, how you’re going to get there, what you’re going to eat, and how you’re going to continue your journey.And if you’re somewhere you never intended to visit, you may not know anything about the surrounding area.That’s where we found ourselves.We hadn’t researched Wilkes-Barre because there was no reason to research Wilkes-Barre. We hadn’t selected a hotel based on its proximity to restaurants or entertainment. We didn’t have a list of attractions to visit or a collection of transportation options ready to go.We were suddenly dealing with a destination that hadn’t existed in our plans a few hours earlier.The whole situation was a reminder that travel doesn’t always care what you’ve arranged. You can have a destination, a schedule, and a perfectly reasonable expectation of how the day is supposed to unfold, and then something outside your control changes everything.The FAA had made its decision, and we had to deal with the consequences.The immediate problem was getting situated.We needed a hotel, and we needed transportation to get there.That brings us to one of the more unusual parts of the entire experience.Sharing a Car with a Completely Random DudeGetting to the Holiday Inn wasn’t exactly a straightforward operation.We somehow ended up sharing a car with a completely random dude.That’s right. After being unexpectedly grounded in a city we never planned to visit, one of the next adventures involved climbing into a vehicle with somebody we didn’t know just to get to the hotel.It wasn’t exactly the glamorous beginning to a Pennsylvania vacation that nobody had requested.Most people imagine arriving somewhere, collecting their luggage, getting into a waiting vehicle, and heading to their hotel. Everything is reasonably organized, and you can concentrate on getting settled.Our experience was a little different.We were trying to sort out transportation in an unfamiliar place, and the solution involved sharing a ride with a stranger.There is something inherently funny about how quickly your expectations change when travel doesn’t go according to plan.Under normal circumstances, you might have a list of requirements for transportation. You want something convenient, comfortable, and reasonably direct. You might compare different options or choose the easiest arrangement.When you’ve just been forced to land somewhere you never intended to visit, the priorities become considerably simpler.Does it get us to the hotel?We weren’t trying to arrange a luxury transportation experience. We just needed to get where we were going.So we shared the car with the random dude and made our way to the Holiday Inn.At least that part worked.We had transportation, we arrived at the hotel, and we could finally concentrate on figuring out the next part of the adventure.Unfortunately, the hotel location was about to introduce us to another problem.The Holiday Inn: Welcome to NowhereThere are hotels that are conveniently located near everything you might need, and then there are hotels where you quickly discover that the surrounding area offers very little in the way of convenient options.The Holiday Inn in Wilkes-Barre was not exactly giving us the impression that we had arrived in the center of a thriving entertainment district.We weren’t expecting the hotel to be surrounded by luxury restaurants and expensive shopping. We just wanted somewhere reasonably convenient to get food and perhaps find something to do.That seemed like a fairly modest expectation.But once we were settled, the immediate problem became apparent.There wasn’t much nearby.This is one of those things that can make a tremendous difference when you’re traveling. If you have a car, you can generally get around the problem. A restaurant might be several miles away, but that’s not necessarily an issue if you can simply drive there.When you don’t have that convenience, location becomes extremely important.A restaurant that is five miles away might as well be on another continent if you don’t have a convenient way to reach it.And that’s essentially how the situation started to feel.We were at the Holiday Inn, but being at the hotel didn’t mean we had easy access to anything else.Finding food was going to require some planning.Finding entertainment would require even more.And getting out of town was becoming a separate transportation challenge.It wasn’t exactly the relaxing experience you imagine when you think about a hotel stay.We hadn’t chosen this location because we wanted to explore Wilkes-Barre. We hadn’t spent weeks researching the surrounding neighborhood. We were there because the FAA had forced an unexpected change in our plans, and we needed somewhere to stay.The hotel was a temporary solution to a problem we hadn’t anticipated.Unfortunately, temporary solutions have a way of becoming considerably less appealing when you discover that everything you need is somewhere else.The Great DoorDash DisappointmentNormally, when you’re staying at a hotel and don’t feel like going anywhere, food delivery is a pretty good option.You open an app, look through the available restaurants, find something that sounds decent, place an order, and wait for dinner to arrive.It’s one of the conveniences that makes traveling easier.You don’t need a car. You don’t need to navigate an unfamiliar area. You don’t have to figure out where restaurants are located or how far away they might be.Unfortunately, DoorDash wasn’t going to provide the easy solution we were hoping for.The nearby options weren’t particularly useful, and the entire process became another reminder that we weren’t staying somewhere especially convenient.We weren’t looking for anything complicated. We didn’t need some exclusive dining experience or a restaurant with a celebrity chef.A pizza would have been fine. A decent sandwich would have been fine. Something delivered to the hotel without requiring an elaborate transportation arrangement would have been even better.But apparently, even that was going to be difficult.The delivery situation wasn’t helping, and the nearby restaurant situation wasn’t much better.Eventually, we had to accept that if we wanted dinner, we were going to have to go out and find it ourselves.A Mile for Dinner: The Wilkes-Barre Walking Tour Nobody RequestedThere are plenty of reasons to take a walk when you’re traveling.You might be exploring a new city, enjoying the scenery, checking out interesting neighborhoods, or simply getting some exercise.Walking a mile because there is nowhere convenient to get dinner is a different experience.That’s what we ended up doing.Approximately one mile just to find something to eat.It sounds almost ridiculous when you think about it. We were staying at a hotel, and rather than having a selection of restaurants nearby, we had to make a fairly substantial walk to locate somewhere to eat.Nobody was asking for a five-star dining experience. We weren’t trying to discover some hidden culinary destination. We just wanted a meal.The problem was that the immediate area wasn’t giving us many options.And eventually found an Italian restaurant.At that point, we were hoping that the effort would be worthwhile. After everything that had happened, a decent dinner would have been a welcome improvement.We had already been forced to land in an unexpected city, dealt with transportation problems, shared a car with a random stranger, and discovered that our hotel wasn’t particularly convenient for finding food.Surely dinner could go right.Surely we could have one ordinary, enjoyable experience.Wilkes-Barre had one more surprise waiting.The Italian Restaurant: Twenty Dollars for Something from the Frozen Food SectionThe Italian restaurant deserves its own section because the meal was almost too ridiculous to forget.After walking approximately a mile, we finally arrived at a place that looked like it might provide a reasonable dinner.Italian food is generally a pretty dependable choice. You can find good Italian restaurants in almost any city, and even a relatively simple restaurant can serve a satisfying meal.Pasta, sauce, perhaps some chicken, and a little bread.It isn’t exactly rocket science.We weren’t expecting an elaborate dining experience. We just wanted something that tasted like it had been prepared in an actual restaurant.Instead, we ended up with what was essentially a Lean Cuisine for $20.Those little frozen meals you find in the grocery store. The ones you purchase when you’re too tired to cook, take home, put in the microwave, and eat while wondering why you didn’t just order a pizza.That was essentially the experience.Except this version required walking a mile, sitting in a restaurant, and paying approximately $20.There is something particularly insulting about spending restaurant money on food that looks like it should come with instructions telling you to remove the plastic film before microwaving.You almost have to admire the accomplishment.We had gone through all the trouble of finding the place, getting there, sitting down, ordering, and waiting for dinner.And after all that, we were left with something that probably would have been just as satisfying if we’d purchased it at Walmart.At least we could have eaten it in the hotel room without making the one-mile journey.The entire experience became another example of how nothing about the Wilkes-Barre portion of the trip seemed to be working in our favor.The transportation was inconvenient.The hotel location wasn’t particularly useful.DoorDash wasn’t solving the problem.And when we finally found a restaurant, the meal wasn’t worth the effort.At this point, Wilkes-Barre was building a pretty impressive record.We had arrived there against our wishes, and the town seemed to be doing everything possible to make sure we didn’t develop any affection for it.The food certainly wasn’t helping.And then Saturday night arrived.Saturday Night: We Just Wanted Something to DoThere is something particularly disappointing about spending a Saturday night somewhere and discovering that you have absolutely no interest in any of the available entertainment options.When you’re traveling, Saturday night is usually an opportunity to get out and enjoy yourself.You might find a bar, catch some live music, visit a restaurant, or simply walk around and see what’s happening.It doesn’t have to be complicated.Sometimes the best part of traveling is discovering something you weren’t expecting.A great little restaurant, a local music venue, an interesting neighborhood, or a bar where you end up spending several hours having a good time.We were hoping for something along those lines.Instead, we were in Wilkes-Barre.And we were desperate to find something to do.Not looking for one or two possibilities.We genuinely wanted to get out of the hotel and do something entertaining.After everything else that had happened, we were ready for a little normality.A decent bar would have been fine.Live music would have been great.A restaurant with some atmosphere would have worked.Even a place to grab a drink and sit around for a while would have been an improvement.But we searched and searched, and there was absolutely nothing that seemed worth the effort.You know how sometimes you search for things to do in a city and find dozens of possibilities?You start narrowing them down.Maybe this place looks interesting. Maybe that bar has live music. Maybe there’s an event happening downtown.We weren’t having that experience.We were struggling to find even one thing that made us want to leave the hotel.And the more we looked, the more absurd the situation became.We had been forced to land in a city we never intended to visit.And now we couldn’t even find anything entertaining to do.At some point, you stop wondering what you’re missing and start accepting that the options simply aren’t appealing.Wilkes-Barre was not exactly making a strong case for itself as a weekend destination.The Sharter Show: Our Saturday Night EntertainmentWe had searched for something to do, considered the possibilities, and reached the conclusion that there was absolutely nothing worth going out for.And that’s how we ended up watching the Sharter Show.After everything involved in getting to Wilkes-Barre, our Saturday-night entertainment consisted of watching television in the hotel room.It’s difficult to imagine a more appropriate ending to the day.We hadn’t chosen to stay in because we were exhausted from an exciting day of sightseeing. We weren’t relaxing after visiting a collection of interesting attractions.We were simply out of options.There was nothing we wanted to go see, nowhere we particularly wanted to visit, and no compelling reason to leave the hotel.So we watched the Sharter Show.If somebody had told us at the beginning of the trip that this would be how we spent Saturday night, it probably would have sounded like a joke.We were supposed to be traveling from Rochester to Atlanta.Instead, we were grounded in Wilkes-Barre, walking a mile for dinner, paying $20 for a frozen-food-quality Italian meal, and watching the Sharter Show because the town had apparently run out of entertainment.It’s the kind of thing you can’t really plan.And it’s also the kind of thing that makes a trip memorable.The funny part is that we weren’t even particularly difficult to entertain. We weren’t demanding a major concert or a professional sporting event.We just wanted something to do.Instead, Saturday night ended up being a hotel-room television experience.At least we had something to laugh about.Operation: Get Us Out of Wilkes-BarreBy this point, the biggest priority was finding a way to leave.We had never intended to be there, and the longer the situation continued, the more we wanted to move on.The original journey was Rochester to Atlanta. That was where we were supposed to be going.Wilkes-Barre was an interruption, not a destination.And it was becoming an interruption that was difficult to get past.The transportation situation made everything more complicated.We didn’t have a convenient car sitting outside the hotel. We couldn’t simply get in and drive to another city. We didn’t have an easy train option that would solve the problem, and flying wasn’t going to provide a practical answer to every short-distance transportation question.We were left looking at whatever options were available.And when you’re stuck somewhere you don’t want to be, you become considerably less particular about how you leave.Normally, you might compare transportation options based on comfort, schedule, convenience, and cost.At this point, the criteria were much simpler.Does it get us out of Wilkes-Barre?The idea of taking a bus became part of the discussion.And not necessarily some luxurious bus experience with comfortable seats and a relaxing journey.We were even considering a bus with a bunch of older passengers.At that point, who cared?If it got us somewhere else, it was worth considering.There is a certain desperation involved in reaching the point where you’re willing to accept almost any reasonable transportation arrangement simply because you want to leave.We weren’t looking for a sightseeing tour.We weren’t trying to experience the local transportation system for fun.We were looking for an escape route.The Bus with the Older PassengersThe bus idea deserves a mention because it illustrates just how far the transportation situation had drifted from the original plan.Think about the journey we had started with.Somewhere along the way, the FAA forced us to land in Wilkes-Barre, and now we were considering a bus with a group of older passengers as a possible way to get moving again.It’s not exactly the kind of transportation planning you see in travel brochures.Nobody starts a trip thinking, “I really hope I get to spend part of this adventure figuring out whether I can get on a bus with a bunch of older people.”But that’s what happens when the usual transportation options aren’t available.You start looking at alternatives.And then you start looking at alternatives to the alternatives.Eventually, almost anything that gets you out of the situation becomes interesting.The whole thing was particularly frustrating because none of this was part of our original plan.We hadn’t chosen to spend time in Wilkes-Barre. We hadn’t booked the Holiday Inn because we wanted to explore the surrounding area. We hadn’t researched restaurants or entertainment.We were simply trying to continue a journey that had been interrupted.And every time we thought we had found a way forward, another transportation question seemed to appear.It was becoming less about enjoying the trip and more about managing the logistics.Still, there was one unexpected bright spot in the middle of all this.A Surprise Worth Leaving the Hotel For: Arrested DevelopmentSomehow, we managed to catch Arrested Development.And unlike the Italian restaurant, this was a discovery that actually turned out to be worthwhile.The group became one of the most distinctive names in hip-hop during the early 1990s, arriving at a time when the genre was expanding in several different directions.Their debut album, 3 Years, 5 Months and 2 Days in the Life Of…, introduced a sound that was considerably different from much of the hardcore rap and gangsta rap that dominated the conversation during that period.Led by Speech, Arrested Development combined hip-hop with elements of funk, soul, gospel, and socially conscious songwriting.Songs like “Tennessee,” “People Everyday,” and “Mr. Wendal” helped establish the group as a major name in alternative hip-hop.The group was particularly interesting because it didn’t follow the same formula as many of its contemporaries. Their music had a different perspective, a different sound, and a different approach to the subject matter.They were part of a movement that demonstrated just how broad hip-hop could be.Their success was significant, and their debut album received widespread recognition. The group eventually became one of the defining acts of the alternative hip-hop movement.Catching them during this unexpected journey was a nice surprise.It wasn’t something we had planned around the trip. We hadn’t set out to see Arrested Development. We were simply making the most of whatever opportunities came along.And after the transportation headaches, disappointing food, and Saturday-night entertainment disaster, a live music opportunity was certainly welcome.It was also a reminder that unexpected detours aren’t always bad.Sometimes you end up discovering something worthwhile in the middle of an otherwise ridiculous experience.Arrested Development gave us one of those moments.And it was considerably better than watching the Sharter Show.Hip-Hop Was an Unexpected HighlightThere is something particularly enjoyable about seeing a band or artist you weren’t necessarily expecting to see.When you plan a concert trip around a particular performer, you know what you’re getting into. You research the setlists, look at the venue, and anticipate the songs you hope to hear.When a concert happens unexpectedly, the experience can be different.You might not know exactly what the performance will be like. You might not have been following the artist particularly closely. You simply recognize an opportunity and decide to take advantage of it.That was the appeal of catching Arrested Development.Their music occupies an interesting place in hip-hop history.The early 1990s were an important period for the genre. Rap was becoming increasingly mainstream, but there was also a tremendous amount of experimentation happening outside the biggest commercial acts.Some groups focused on harder-edged street narratives. Others explored jazz, funk, soul, political commentary, or more personal songwriting.Arrested Development stood out because of its combination of musical influences and positive, socially conscious perspective.“Tennessee” remains one of the group’s most recognizable recordings. “People Everyday” demonstrated its ability to take an existing musical idea and transform it into something distinctly its own. “Mr. Wendal” offered a different perspective on homelessness and social inequality.These weren’t simply songs designed to fit into a particular commercial trend.They helped establish an identity.And seeing a group with that kind of history was a nice addition to a trip that had already taken several unexpected turns.It was one of those moments where you could stop thinking about the transportation problems for a while and simply enjoy the music.That was something we could certainly use.The Strange Economics of Being Stuck SomewhereOne thing you quickly discover when travel plans go wrong is that even ordinary activities become more expensive and inconvenient.When you’re in a familiar city, you know where things are. You might have friends nearby, transportation options you understand, and a general idea of where to go for food.When you’re unexpectedly stranded somewhere, you lose much of that familiarity.You don’t necessarily know which restaurants are good, which neighborhoods are convenient, or how to get around.You start making decisions based on limited information.And sometimes those decisions turn out to be terrible.The Italian restaurant was a perfect example.We needed food, the options were limited, and we eventually walked a mile to find something that sounded reasonably appealing.And then we realized that the entire experience had been a waste of time compared with what we could have done if we had been somewhere with better options.The $20 Lean Cuisine became a symbol of the entire Wilkes-Barre experience.It wasn’t just about the food.It was about the effort required to find it, the lack of alternatives, and the disappointment of finally getting somewhere only to discover that it wasn’t worth the trouble.The same thing happened with entertainment.We wanted to go out Saturday night, but the options weren’t appealing.We spent time searching, trying to find something, and eventually gave up.When you’re traveling, time is valuable. You don’t want to spend an entire evening researching activities that you probably won’t enjoy.You want to be out experiencing something.Unfortunately, that wasn’t how the Wilkes-Barre portion of the trip unfolded.A City We Never Intended to VisitThe biggest irony is that Wilkes-Barre never had to impress us.We hadn’t chosen it as a destination.We weren’t expecting to spend a vacation there.We didn’t have a bucket list of attractions to visit.We were simply there because the FAA forced the aircraft to land.That distinction is important.This wasn’t a situation where we researched the city, decided it looked interesting, and then became disappointed when it didn’t meet our expectations.We never wanted to be there in the first place.And after spending time trying to navigate the transportation situation, find food, and locate entertainment, we weren’t developing any new appreciation for the place.If anything, we were becoming increasingly motivated to leave.The town had managed to turn a straightforward journey into an unexpected collection of logistical problems.And while there may be plenty of people who enjoy living in Wilkes-Barre, our particular experience wasn’t giving us many reasons to become enthusiastic visitors.The transportation problems were frustrating.The hotel location was inconvenient.The food was disappointing.Saturday-night entertainment was practically nonexistent from our perspective.And the only reason we were there was because the FAA had made the landing necessary.It was an unwanted stop that became a much bigger part of the journey than anybody could have anticipated.Looking Back at the Whole ExperienceWhen you look back at a trip like this, it’s interesting how the memories become organized.You might initially remember the inconvenience, the frustration, and the amount of time spent trying to figure out what to do next.But eventually, those experiences become stories.The random guy who shared the car ride.The Holiday Inn with practically nothing nearby.The mile-long walk for dinner.The Italian restaurant that served a $20 Lean Cuisine.The Saturday night when we couldn’t find anything to do.The idea of taking a bus with a bunch of older passengers just to get out of town.And then the unexpected opportunity to catch Arrested Development.It’s a pretty unusual collection of memories.None of them was part of the original plan, but all of them became part of the trip.And perhaps that’s what makes the story so memorable.We didn’t set out to create an elaborate travel adventure. We were simply trying to get from Rochester to Atlanta.Wilkes-Barre became an unexpected stop, and everything that followed was an exercise in improvisation.Final Thoughts: The FAA Owed Us a Better DestinationTravel is supposed to be about getting somewhere, discovering new places, and enjoying experiences along the way.Sometimes it works out perfectly.And sometimes the FAA forces you to land in Wilkes-Barre, and suddenly the entire trip becomes an exercise in figuring out how to survive the unexpected detour.We started out in Rochester with Atlanta as the destination.Instead, we found ourselves in a city we never planned to visit, sharing a car with a random stranger, staying at a Holiday Inn with very little nearby, and trying to find basic conveniences that should have been considerably easier to locate.We walked a mile for dinner and received a $20 meal that resembled a Lean Cuisine.We couldn’t find a decent DoorDash solution.Saturday night offered so little entertainment that we eventually watched the Sharter Show.We desperately looked for ways to get out of town, even considering a bus with a bunch of older passengers.And somehow, through all of this, we managed to catch Arrested Development.There were certainly worse ways to spend an unexpected detour, but there were also considerably better ones.The best part is that we never intended any of it to happen.We weren’t planning a Pennsylvania vacation. We weren’t looking for an opportunity to explore Wilkes-Barre. We weren’t trying to discover its restaurants or nightlife.We were trying to get to Atlanta.Instead, the FAA made Wilkes-Barre part of our story, and the town did not exactly make a convincing argument for extending the visit.If nothing else, we learned a few things.First, always appreciate having transportation available. You never know when you’ll find yourself somewhere you didn’t intend to visit and suddenly have to investigate every possible way of getting out.Second, research the hotel location whenever possible. Being close to a hotel doesn’t necessarily mean being close to anything useful.Third, don’t assume that an Italian restaurant will provide a decent meal. Sometimes a $20 Lean Cuisine is exactly what you’re going to get, only with a longer walk and a much larger bill.Fourth, Saturday night entertainment is not guaranteed. Sometimes you can search and search and still come up empty.And finally, if you’re sitting in a hotel room watching the Sharter Show because you’ve run out of things to do, perhaps it’s time to reconsider your current location.We never asked for a Wilkes-Barre vacation.We didn’t book it, plan it, or choose it.And after everything we experienced, I think we can safely say that it wasn’t exactly the destination we would have selected ourselves.At least we got to see Arrested Development along the way.The original plan was Rochester to Atlanta.The actual adventure was a forced landing, a transportation nightmare, a disappointing Italian dinner, an entertainment drought, and an unexpected concert.Not exactly what we had in mind.But certainly a story worth telling.And if anyone ever asks whether we would recommend spending a weekend in Wilkes-Barre, the answer might depend on how much they enjoy walking a mile for a $20 frozen dinner and watching the Sharter Show on Saturday night.Personally, I’d rather take my chances with the FAA.

item.title: DC votes for the Royals Hall of Fame, Part 1
item.author: SRS0=+its=JF=mg-d0.substack.com=bounce+9ddca1.63af5d-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: Now that the dust has settled from the 2026 mid-terms, we can turn our attention to another election chock full of debate and controversy…the election for the Royals Hall of Fame Class of 2027.This is the first time we are seeing some of the names from the ‘14 and ‘15 teams on the ballot, it will be fascinating to see who gets the nod and who doesn’t. Royals Hall of Fame Voting (Regular Phase) - 2027 Rules and Guidelines for EligibilityRoyals Hall of Fame Voting (Regular Phase) shall be completed annually with electors consisting of the following: (1) All living members of the Royals Hall of Fame (2) Royals Ownership (3) Members of the Royals Hall of Fame Executive Board (4) Royals Associates with 15 years or more service (5) Select members of the Kansas City Chapter of the Baseball Writers of America and Kansas City media members (6) Royals Fans to be represented as twelve electors via on-line balloting (Fan Vote Distribution: twelve full votes for each of the top five vote getters).To be eligible for the first time Royals Alumni must have been active in the Major Leagues at some time during a period beginning twelve (12) years before and ending three (3) years or more prior to election. Eligible alumni that received a minimum of ten percent (10%) of the vote in the most recent prior election cycle remain on the ballot for up to five cycles. All eligible alumni must have been active with the Kansas City Royals for at least three (3) seasons and accumulated a minimum of 1,500 plate appearances or 300 innings pitched; managers must have led the Royals for at least the equivalent of three full seasons. Those eligible shall have ceased to be an active on-field member of the Kansas City Royals (or for any other Major League Organization) in the role for which they are being considered for at least three (3) calendar years preceding the election – but may be otherwise connected to the Royals or another Major League Organization.Any eligible alumni receiving votes on seventy-five percent (75%) of the ballots cast will be deemed an elected Royals Hall of Fame member. To remain on the ballot for the next RHOF voting cycle, eligible alumni must receive a minimum of ten percent (10%) of the ballots cast. In even numbered years, at the discretion of the Royals Hall of Fame Executive Board, a separate Veterans Committee vote can consider the candidacy of non-player personnel and alumni who previously received Royals Hall of Fame Voting (Regular Phase) votes but are no longer eligible for election in that manner. —- from www.royals.comThere are 12 players on the ballot, you can vote for up to 5. First let’s look at the two players on the ballot for the final time… Combine that production with the effortless outfield defense he played during the first half of his career and you have one of the best all around baseball players of this century. The Baseball Writers of America recognized that by voting Beltran into the Baseball Hall of Fame last summer. Batting Average - 3rd (.295)On-base Percentage - 6th (.359)Slugging Percentage - 7th (.449)There’s absolutely no denying that Billy Butler is in a group with Hal McRae, Mike Sweeney, and now Bobby Witt Jr as the greatest right-handed hitters in club history. There’s also no sane way to justify not voting Butler into the Royals Hall of Fame. Besides, the guy has the best nickname in team history. Who doesn’t like a big helping of Country Breakfast? There are four players on the Royals Hall of Fame ballot for the first time this year. Let’s look at each of them, and we’ll cover the other 6 returning names on the ballot next time.Hosmer was a very good player in Kansas City, albeit with some holes in his game that he never really closed up. Take a look at the 8 offensive categories I listed for Butler above. In how many of those categories do you think Hosmer ranks above Butler? Hosmer and Butler are tied with 127 homers as a Royal, otherwise Butler clears Hoz in every category. Hosmer was also unquestionably the leader of the ‘14 and ‘15 squads, and that’s what tips the scales for me. It might come as a surprise to some, but I’m a YES on Hosmer for the Royals Hall of Fame. Here’s the important thing….if you vote for Hosmer you absolutely have to vote for Butler as well. Before we move on, let me share my favorite Hosmer clip….Moose also authored one of the greatest post-season plays of all time in Game 3 of the 2014 ALCS… I’m a NO on him for the HOFOk, that leaves 6 more players to discuss, all of whom have been on the ballot before. We’ll talk about Lorenzo Cain, Alcides Escobar, Joakim Soria, Greg Holland, Wade Davis, and Kelvin Herrera in the next edition of the Diamond Chronicles!

item.title: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2:Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have"Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view.I also had Claude build a comprehensive demo which works in the latest Datasette Lite, so you can visit this link to load the plugin and a demo database in your browser via Pyodide and WebAssembly.I like this demo page showing both GeoJSON shapes and lat/lon points on the same map:

item.title: datasette 1.0a43
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone, which is now 53% complete.There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory: private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed).The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: no-preference auto facet-results rows-tableWith that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.)

item.title: Jensen Huang’s Role: A Different Picture Comes Into Focus
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I don’t want to make too much of a single report. But I’m flagging it here because it fits with a number of other emerging data points about the NVIDIA-Huang scandal. What are those emerging data points? I’d describe them broadly as suggesting there was at least as much push from NVIDIA/Huang to keep selling its chips into China, in the face of tightening export controls, as there was intelligence skullduggery by China to bring them into the country. In that context, Alice Huang seems as much an intermediary or partner as a spy or trickster pulling anything over on anyone.The report comes from CBS News and it was published late Friday evening.

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes' fiance is the worst man in America. Now we have him on tape.
item.content:encoded: NOTE: This review contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”Sometimes the best journalists are people who don’t even purport to be journalists. The late Anthony Bourdain was one such accidental herald, as was “Borat” star Sacha Baron Cohen before the gonzo comedian became recognizably famous no matter his alter ego. Let’s go ahead and add writer/performer Nathan Fielder to the list. You and I know Fielder best from “Nathan For You” and “The Rehearsal.” Everyone else is about to know him for “You Can See Everything,” a tag team effort with documentarian Lance Oppenheim that is not only the best film of 2026 so far, but also one of the finest works of journalism I’ve ever seen.This movie arrives in theaters with plenty of deserved Oscar buzz. But in this case, a mere filmmaking award seems insufficient in recognition. As far as I’m concerned, this thing deserves a Pulitzer (categories be damned). And maybe a Nobel Prize.Article continues below this adBut I’m getting ahead of myself. In case you haven’t seen the film’s trailer, “You Can See Everything” is a portrait of infamous Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted in 2022 of defrauding her company’s investors and is currently in prison in Texas. You can read all about Holmes in John Carreyrou’s book “Bad Blood,” an essential tick-tock of the Theranos scandal. The book not only tells the story of how Holmes led people to believe that her company’s revolutionary blood-testing hardware worked (it did not), but also of how the greater Silicon Valley culture inspired Holmes, and in some cases perhaps abetted her. The Theranos scandal was one of the highest profile financial scandals of this century, and Holmes was the haunting, unblinking face of it.Holmes went dark for years after her malfeasance was exposed, until she and her fiance, Billy Evans, agreed to let Fielder and Oppenheim into their slipshod rental cottage in Del Mar for weeks on end and film the couple (and their two very cute children) as they prepared for Holmes to report to prison. Fielder and Oppenheim were allowed to film the Holmes family nearly 24/7, with Fielder at one point agreeing to stay with the family for an extended period of time. Hence, the film’s title. You will, indeed, see everything. Almost too much of everything, given that this doc runs nearly three hours, and given that the camera stays uncomfortably tight on its participants, Fielder included, for the bulk of that time.You’ll also see Billy Evans’ penis, so be warned or titillated as you see fit.Article continues below this adAs Fielder ingratiates himself with Holmes and Evans, he gets them comfortable enough to ask the hard questions: about Theranos, about prison, and even about themselves. The resulting footage is often shocking. You will see Elizabeth Holmes, who still maintains she did nothing wrong, answer “no” when Fielder asks her if she’s ever lied in her life. You will hear Billy Evans, the real villain in this particular story, tell everyone in the room that he carries a gun on him 24/7. You will see Fielder screen the legendary “Who’s on first?” sketch for Holmes and her partner, with Holmes missing the central joke of the sketch entirely. You will see Fielder explain to Holmes that “Who” is the name of the guy on first base, with her still not really grasping it. And you’ll see Holmes’ partner tell her, “You see the world differently,” in a skin-crawling attempt to turn her seeming cluelessness into something laudatory. The Silicon Valley mindset at work.Speaking of the Valley mindset, you will also see Holmes and Evans spend a great deal of time in this movie attempting to boot up Theranos 2.0. They even go so far as to drag out some of the original Theranos blood testing apparatus, which looks like a bunch of random parts from TigerDirect they hooked together, to show Fielder what their product can do. We do not see it doing anything on screen, but the couple assures that it would if it was, like, hooked up properly. These scenes are extremely funny, but funny isn’t what Fielder is looking for. He’s trying to figure out if this woman is a clueless naif, if she believes her own lies, or if she is playing the of an innocent woman, and doing so with such effectiveness that, to paraphrase Fielder, she might be the most manipulative person in the world.Article continues below this adThe answer proves fabulously elusive, and so Fielder and Oppenheim go to extremes in their attempt to find it. They hold the camera on Holmes’ rubbery elfin face for what feels like hours at a time, to see if she’ll blink (figuratively literally!). They interview Holmes’ visiting parents, with the father, former Enron exec Christian Holmes, casually telling Fielder that everything changed for his daughter “when she was raped.” To the furthest extreme, they bring in actress Amanda Seyfried — who Holmes in the Hulu TV show “The Dropout” — to recreate any dialogues Fielder had with Holmes herself that couldn’t be recorded on camera. Seyfried is so convincing in mimicking Holmes that you, the audience, might forget which scenes were Seyfried talking to the camera and not Holmes herself. I know I did.It gets crazier. After Holmes reports to prison, Seyfried joins Fielder on a trip to visit Billy Evans in a clandestine attempt to get Holmes’ partner to admit that, without Holmes’ knowledge, he demanded (and for a moment, received promise of), monetary compensation from the A24 studio for the couple’s participation in this documentary.A brief pause here. Billy Evans is scion to the San Diego-based Evans Hotels family fortune. Evans met Holmes well after she’d become notorious, but tells Fielder early in “You Can See Everything” that he didn’t recognize her when the two first met. In fact, he fell in love with Holmes within an hour of meeting her, then found out who she was, still wanted to be with her anyway. Do you buy this story? Of course you don’t. This man is full of s—t, and that becomes even more apparent when he’s confronted by both Fielder and Seyfried after Holmes has reported to prison. That’s when we hear Evans sneer, “I’m better read than you,” at Seyfried — who, as a reminder, is one of the most skilled people in the world at her chosen profession. He also taunts Seyfried for getting “owned” on Twitter after she derided the late white supremacist Charlie Kirk, whom of course Evans actually admired. This man is an absolute piece of s—t.Thankfully, Seyfried says as much, becoming audience surrogate after that alarming sequence and telling Fielder that Holmes’ partner is “bats—t crazy.” Amanda Seyfried might be the coolest person in Hollywood. As for Fielder, he’s left wondering if Holmes has been victimized by her own partner, by her former Theranos paramour Sunny Balwani (also now in prison, and whom Holmes also accused of raping her), and by God knows who else. Was this woman, once a billionaire, more pawn than mastermind? Fielder shows some (platonic) fondness for Holmes over the course of this film, but by this point in the story it’s hard to know if , the interviewer, is also playing a character in order to get what he wants.Article continues below this adFielder, to his credit, acknowledges the thorniness of all this. He’s openly uncertain of having Seyfried dramatize Holmes’ words on camera because, no matter how talented the actress is, it’s still not Holmes herself saying those words to the camera. He also doesn’t know if he’s surreptitiously fallen for Holmes’ graciousness, to the point where he questions himself to Seyfried for believing Holmes when she told him, almost on a lark, that she had no clue Evans was making money moves behind her back. That leads to Seyfried herself wondering if her own Hulu portrayal of Holmes was truth, blurred truth, or just fiction. By the end of the film, Seyfried isn’t sure what the word “fiction” should even mean.That’s what makes this film a masterwork. “You Can See Everything” refers plainly to the extensive footage that Fielder and Oppenheim were able to obtain. But here’s a documentary that also shows you, the audience, its whole methodology. It allows you to see the potential flaws in its reporting, and how those flaws might impede the filmmakers’ attempt to find real answers. It’s that truly radical transparency that differentiates this documentary not only from the tacit sponcon docs that now plague your television (Billy Evans cites Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s deal with Netflix as a reason that he should be paid by A24 for appearing on camera), but also from a lot of the best pure documentaries ever filmed. Here is a movie that exists on a level with Banksy’s “Exit Through the Gift Shop” as a superlative example of how the truth can be not just impossible to find but, with great determination, can be eradicated altogether. I’ll never forget it.Article continues below this ad

item.title: Wake Forest Really Kicked Some Ass
item.author: Israel Daramola
item.content:encoded: While prognosticators have been wondering who could be the next school to make an Indiana-type leap into the big leagues, with some already crowning UCLA as the likeliest successor, the Wake Forest Demon Deacons have been quietly developing into something of a budding juggernaut. Those are big words for an ACC program that put up back-to-back 4-8 seasons in 2023 and '24, but I don't think they're totally inaccurate.In Jake Dickert's first year at the helm of Wake Forest, they went 9-4 with a Mayo Bowl win over Mississippi State. In his second year, they are currently 9-1, with their only loss coming against championship favorite Miami. While they have not exactly gone against a gauntlet, they have dominated in most of their games, particularly in the last six weeks, outscoring their opponents 313-38.This casualty list added SMU on Saturday when the Demon Deacons crushed the Mustangs 49-7, with 42 points scored in the first half. It was a spanking! Quarterback Gio Lopez accounted for 201 yards and a TD in the air, plus 34 yards and two more TDs on the ground, while the running backs added another 252 yards and four TDs. SMU, which is a good team with a solid record, could do absolutely nothing against these guys. They committed three turnovers and were not able to score until garbage time in the third quarter.

item.title: Here’s The Latest Stupid Way That The NHL Is Messing With Its Broadcasts
item.author: Lauren Theisen
item.content:encoded: The NHL unveiled a whole roster of alternate jerseys for this season, and the Tampa Bay Lightning's features a big skull, which you can see at center ice in the above screenshot. At first, I wondered if it was just some synergy with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, but I have since learned that it's a tribute to the city's annual Gasparilla Season, which is headlined by a pirate parade with a fraught racial past.But does that center-ice logo look kind of uncanny to you? Maybe a little too smooth or artificial? Honestly, does it even look like ice at all? Watch the players skate over it, and see for yourself. https://youtu.be/qnRrDN5X6Sw?si=9kRmnHllEIwtvcXm&t=231

item.title: Texas And LSU Had A Barnburner Of Dumbass Football
item.author: Israel Daramola
item.content:encoded: The Texas Longhorns triumphed in an exciting, last-second 22-21 victory over the LSU Tigers on Saturday, thanks to a heroic effort by QB Arch Manning and some typical breaking down of the LSU defense. But if you did not watch the contest in full, do not let the thrilling end fool you: This was some of the year's dumbest football, authored by two of our dumbest college football programs.Let's start with the six interceptions total in this game: three for each, which is nice and neat. At first, it was LSU's Sam Leavitt throwing most of the picks, two in the first half, which makes it particularly strange that LSU was leading for the majority of this game. They were helped by the fact that Manning tossed two picks in the second half, to add to one he threw in the second quarter, and as a result the game was the Tigers' for the taking—21-10 late in the third, and still 21-16 when they punted with only 2:19 to go.But if nothing else, Manning has shown an ability to get better when his back is against the wall. And if you're going to beat Texas, you have to stomp them out completely. Despite Manning's overall pedestrian performance, 174 yards on 19 of 35 passes, his night climaxed with the crucial touchdown. In the game's final two minutes, Manning led a 12-play, 58-yard drive down the field, culminating in a seven-yard run on third down at LSU's 11-yard line and then a four-yard TD pass to RB Raleek Brown for the go-ahead score. Cue the Texas sideline going absolutely, understandably nuts.

item.title: Did Ole Miss Simply Lack The Grit To Get To Their Game On Time?
item.author: Lauren Theisen
item.content:encoded: On Friday, a nationwide ground stop lasting over four hours led to thousands of flight cancellations and delays from coast to coast. As a result, we're getting some Sunday afternoon college football, with No. 19 Ole Miss playing Oklahoma in Norman because they couldn't arrive on their previous schedule.Per Ole Miss, who was flying out of Tupelo, about 50 miles from their campus in Oxford, the ground stop began just a few minutes before the team buses were scheduled to leave for the airport, at 4 p.m. Once they learned that the stop would last for hours, the players were allowed to go, and they were called for a team meeting at 8 p.m., just a little before stop was lifted. Still, it was apparently too late for them to salvage their journey that night, and the SEC ultimately pushed the game back a day as a result."At that hour, due to the time required to rescreen the party and travel to the Tupelo airport, the crew's duty time would have expired prior to departure," the Ole Miss statement said. "There were no other flight options at that point, and we determined it was too late to put our student-athletes on a bus trip of eight or more hours. In addition, the flight crew's duty time restrictions prevented us from being able to fly out until Saturday afternoon at the earliest."
